data.title: Alexandr Wang, el joven prodigio de la IA de Meta
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta's AI director, led the launch of Muse Wonder, which boosted the company's stock and his reputation. The move follows Muse's viral success as the top free app, and Wang is now seen as a potential successor to Zuckerberg.
data.author: Rafe Rosner-Uddin
data.full_text:
TECNOLOGÍA Alexandr Wang, el joven prodigio de la IA de Meta Alexandr Wang. Bloomberg Seguir a Expansión en Google Haz que nuestras noticias aparezcan en tus búsquedas Zuckerberg rechaza frenar la IA: "Meta ha alcanzado a sus rivales"

Meta: al ataque del club de los dos billones aupada por Muse A sus 29 años, el director de los laboratorios de superinteligencia de la compañía está considerado como un posible sucesor de Mark Zuckerberg.

A finales del año pasado, cuando Alexandr Wang tuvo que informar a los ejecutivos de Meta sobre el progreso de la apuesta de la empresa por la IA, un plan decisivo para su futuro, Wang optó por presentar un “informe de impresiones” que apenas contenía detalles. La reunión no tranquilizó a la directora financiera, Susan Li: “Si esto no funciona, las consecuencias serán muy, muy graves en términos financieros”, declaró Li. Pero el lunes de la semana pasada, Wang pudo ofrecer a Li y al resto de los presentes pruebas claras de que esta inversión multimillonaria está dando sus frutos: el lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA Muse Wonder de Meta hizo subir las acciones de la compañía, y con ello, la reputación de Wang. El joven de 29 años - al frente de los laboratorios de superinteligencia de Meta y cuya costosa contratación, derivada de una operación de 14.300 millones de dólares que también involucró a su empresa de etiquetado de datos Scale AI- causó sorpresa el año pasado, ha saltado a la fama y es ahora aclamado como el hombre que ha devuelto a Meta a la carrera por la IA. La app más descargada Según Mark Zuckerberg, el lanzamiento de Muse Wonder ha devuelto a Meta a la vanguardia de la IA. Esto ha ocurrido apenas cinco semanas después de que el nuevo agente de IA de Meta, Muse, experimentara un éxito viral que lo convirtió en la aplicación gratuita más descargada en las tiendas de aplicaciones de Apple y Android. El jueves de la semana pasada, Wang también anunció que Meta iba a asociarse con Apple para implementar sus modelos de IA de “pesos abiertos” en los ordenadores Mac. Wang creció en Nuevo México y es hijo de dos físicos chinoestadounidenses. Fue un niño prodigio de las matemáticas: terminó el bachillerato un año antes de lo habitual y se trasladó a Silicon Valley, donde trabajó para el sitio web de preguntas y respuestas Quora. A los 18 años ingresó en el MIT, pero abandonó sus estudios un año después para fundar Scale AI en 2016. Esta compañía, que proporciona datos seleccionados y etiquetados para el entrenamiento de modelos de IA, ha firmado acuerdos con grupos como OpenAI y Anthropic. “Alex no solo es inteligente y tiene una gran capacidad técnica, sino que también destaca por la profundidad de sus análisis y su estilo de comunicación. Es precoz y posee una madurez impropia de su edad”, señala Mike Volpi, uno de los primeros inversores en Scale y socio de la firma de capital riesgo Hanabi Capital. Wang cuenta con una amplia red de contactos en el sector tecnológico (por ejemplo, compartió piso con Sam Altman, de OpenAI). Scale firmó su primer contrato con Facebook en 2019, y Wang conoció a Zuckerberg dos años después. Sin embargo, la relación dio un giro radical el año pasado, tras el lanzamiento por parte de Meta de un nuevo modelo de IA que resultó ser decepcionante. Esto llevó a Zuckerberg a reestructurar el equipo de IA de Meta y a renovar su liderazgo. Wang y Zuckerberg se reunieron varias veces en 2015 para tratar la posibilidad de que el fundador de Scale AI trabajara en Meta. Juntos trazaron una hoja de ruta de un año de duración con el objetivo de devolver a la compañía a la vanguardia de la IA. Según personas cercanas a él, Wang es un “ejecutor” capaz de hablar el mismo lenguaje que los ingenieros de IA. Sin embargo, al entrar en Meta como director de IA se enfrentó a presiones tanto internas como externas, dado que nunca antes había trabajado en el entrenamiento de modelos de IA. Durante sus primeros meses al mando, desató una guerra por el talento en Silicon Valley y contrató a investigadores estrella de la competencia. Pero los primeros modelos lanzados bajo su liderazgo no lograron seguir el ritmo de los de sus rivales. A pesar de ello, seguía contando con toda la atención y el respaldo de Zuckerberg. Anastasios Angelopoulos, CEO de la plataforma abierta para la evaluación de modelos de IA Arena, afirma que Meta ha logrado avances significativos con Wang: “Aún no están al nivel de los modelos de Anthropic y OpenAI, pero los progresos han sido enormes. Y todo es gracias a Alex”. Una persona que ha trabajado tanto con Wang como con Zuckerberg señala las similitudes entre ambos, pero afirma que “Mark tiene una visión mucho más cínica, tanto de su propia perspectiva como de su relevancia y su lugar en la cultura popular. Alex no ha tenido que capear tantas tormentas”. Polémicas Durante el mandato de Wang, Scale se vio envuelta en varias polémicas, entre ellas una demanda en la que se alegaba que la empresa exigía a su personal evaluar material extremo como parte de su trabajo de etiquetado de datos. La demanda fue retirada posteriormente. Además, Wang tuvo enfrentamientos con la cofundadora Lucy Guo, a quien despidió en 2018. No obstante, Wang ha logrado evitar contratiempos de gran repercusión, lo que le ha permitido mantener una imagen pública distendida. Zuckerberg sostiene que Wang es la persona idónea para liderar los planes de Meta en el ámbito de la IA y le otorga un margen de maniobra del que pocos en la empresa disfrutan. Y ya se empieza a considerar a Wang como un posible sucesor de Zuckerberg. ¿Quién es? Desplegable

data.title: Technology increasingly impacting national security: Expert
data.ai_summary: A senior Malaysian official at the Global Security Forum 2026 in Doha said technology is increasingly influencing national security and strategic partnerships, citing access to semiconductors, AI, and critical minerals. He noted Malaysia's semiconductor strategy and ASEAN digital frameworks as key to developing technological capabilities.
data.author: The Peninsula Newspaper

industries.name: Science, Technology & Innovation Administration (National R&D Policy)

company_mentions.name: Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute
Institute of Strategic & International Studies Malaysia

data.full_text:
The Peninsula

Doha: Technology is increasingly influencing national security, economic competitiveness and relations between countries. Access to semiconductors, AI, computing infrastructure and critical minerals is becoming an important consideration in strategic partnerships, said a senior official from Malaysia during a panel discussion at the Global Security Forum 2026 in Doha recently.

Executive Chairman of the Institute of Strategic and International Studies (ISIS) Malaysia Prof. Dr. Mohd Faiz Abdullah participated in a panel discussion entitled “Technology for Development: The Future of Strategic Alliances.” The session also featured Executive Director of Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute Dr. Torek Al Ansori; Professor of International Politics at Georgetown University in Qatar Dr. Roy Miller; and Head of Engineering, EMEA, Scale AI Dr. Hisham Mohamed. The discussion was moderated by Imran Khan, a senior presenter at Al Jazeera Network.

During the session, Dr. Abdullah sharing Malaysia’s perspectives, said, “Malaysia was among the earliest countries to condemn the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia, reaffirming Malaysia’s solidarity with the GCC countries and its support for regional peace and stability.” He added, “Technology is increasingly influencing national security, economic competitiveness and relations between countries. Access to semiconductors, AI, computing infrastructure and critical minerals is becoming an important consideration in strategic partnerships.”

Dr. Abdullah further said, “Malaysia’s National Semiconductor Strategy and New Industrial Master Plan reflect the country’s efforts to develop its own technological capabilities through international cooperation, rather than remain dependent on imported technology.

“Digital sovereignty goes beyond where data is stored. It also involves data protection, cybersecurity, accountability and the ability to choose technology providers. At the regional level, Asean’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) and Asean Regional Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) are important mechanisms for strengthening cooperation and the capabilities of member states.”

The discussion also touched on the challenges faced by emerging economies in balancing technological advancement with national interests, particularly amidst growing competition between major technology powers.

data.title: Panellists At Doha-AIS Underscore Importance Of Predictive Technologies In Crisis Management
data.ai_summary: Panellists at Doha-AIS 2026 emphasized predictive AI and digital innovation to improve crisis response and decision-making. MCIT's Iman al-Kuwari highlighted predictive systems used for crowd management at eight stadiums during the 2022 World Cup, while Cisco's Guy Diedrich noted only 13% of business leaders are fully AI-ready.

industries.name: Decision Optimization & Prescriptive Analytics (OR, simulation, what‑if)
Business Continuity, Crisis Management & Resilience Planning
Scenario Planning, Forecasting Platforms & Planning Intelligence

data.full_text:
Panellists At Doha-AIS Underscore Importance Of Predictive Technologies In Crisis Management
The panellists underscored the importance of beefing up digital innovation and intelligent forecasting mechanisms to substantially improve crisis-response efficiency and advance decision-making frameworks across a variety of critical sectors.
Held at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Center (DECC), the panel discussion brought together a pantheon of officials and technology and digital security specialists who discussed predictive intelligence, crisis leadership, and decision-making superiority. They delved into technological solutions and the strategic thrust toward leveraging AI in crisis management and decision-making processes.
Director of the Digital Innovation Department at Qatar's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) Iman al-Kuwari emphasised the pivotal significance of predictive AI in strengthening decision-making systems and crisis management. She noted that the primary challenges during crises do not stem from a shortage of information, but rather from tight time constraints and rapidly evolving circumstances.
MCIT is committed to furnishing leaders and decision-makers with timely information and mechanisms designed to help them make proactive, well-informed decisions, al-Kuwari underscored, highlighting key integrated capabilities that serve as a model for Qatar's national AI system.
She explained that these capabilities encompass a data fabric, designed to provide reliable, standardised information from various government entities and agencies; a prediction engine, intended to help institutions anticipate future developments with a high degree of confidence; and a decision-making cockpit, designed to steer leaders toward the most accurate options and analyses.
The capabilities also include governance and accountability to ensure human responsibility, auditability, and data protection, alongside interoperability and expertise to bolster government integration and deliver efficient services to citizens and employees, al-Kuwari continued.
Al-Kuwari further highlighted Qatar's substantial achievements in this field, particularly its deployment of predictive systems to manage crowd movements across eight stadiums during the FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022.
The integration of AI into legislative and research processes has also substantially reduced the time required to prepare analyses and responses from days to literally mere minutes, she asserted.
For his part, Postdoctoral Research Fellow at Hamad Bin Khalifa University (HBKU) Dr Mohammad Saleh Ali AlShaikh underscored the importance of addressing operational and cybersecurity challenges. He noted that intelligent systems can effectively monitor unusual situations and help fend off potential cyberattacks targeting or tampering with stadium data.
He added that efforts were being made to bolster routine and predictive maintenance to address dynamic loads and sudden electrical surges, thereby helping ensure the stability of the power supply to data centres.
Research at HBKU focuses on integrating AI with physics to enhance predictive accuracy, safeguard data centre infrastructure, and improve the energy efficiency of graphics processing units (GPUs), central processing units (CPUs), and the electrical grid in a hot climate such as Qatar's, Dr AlShaikh pointed out.
For his part, Cisco Systems Senior Vice-President Dr Guy Diedrich said the world is experiencing an unprecedented pace of technological advancement in AI, stressing that flexibility, chameleon-like adaptability, and a prompt response to technological evolution are fundamental to growth and continuity in the decades ahead.
Rapid advances in AI and quantum technologies are having a direct impact on network infrastructure and cybersecurity, Diedrich remarked, underscoring the acute need to invest in intelligent networks with high levels of security to safeguard against emerging digital risks and challenges at the same pace as these technologies evolve.
Diedrich also highlighted findings from the company's AI Readiness Index, which showed that only about 13 percent of business leaders worldwide are fully prepared to work with AI technologies, despite substantial investment in this vital sector. The findings, he said, underscore the gap between the scale of investment and organisations' actual readiness to adapt to this digital transformation.
Head of Global Defense at Scale AI William Long said AI has become a fundamental pillar of the defence sector and modern warfare, stressing that it is no longer merely an option but an integral part of military strategies that must be adopted to avoid adverse consequences.
He explained that the rapid evolution in the use of AI agents and dynamic planning enables military institutions to integrate multiple models and continually update their assessments, allowing them to address emerging challenges and potential errors with greater flexibility than traditional, static planning approaches.
Long further noted that the most acute challenge lies in accelerating decision-making and processing the immense volume of data and information streaming from sensors without falling prey to strategic miscalculations or overlooking potential points of failure.
Running through October 22, AIS 2026 serves as a forum for exploring ways to leverage AI-powered technologies to support security operations and withstand evolving challenges. The conference thus underscores Qatar's standing and role in bolstering security cooperation at both the regional and global levels.

data.title: AI dealmaking evolves beyond mega rounds as strategic M&A gains momentum – Dealspeak North America
data.ai_summary: AI dealmaking in North America is shifting toward strategic acquisitions, with Nvidia's $12.93bn purchase of Hugging Face and AMD's $8.2bn acquisition of World Labs among recent deals. Mergermarket data shows AI M&A and fundraising volume reached $450bn through September 2026, with traditional M&A accounting for 73% of dollar volume in that period.
data.author: Joshua
data.full_text:
AI dealmaking evolves beyond mega rounds as strategic M&A gains momentum – Dealspeak North America
- Strategic acquisitions now dominate AI deal value
- Buyers target talent, technology gaps, customers
- Funding still drives most AI deal count
AI dealmaking in North America appears to be entering a new phase.
After the enormous venture funding rounds and talent-driven ‘acquihires’ that dominated the last couple of years, recent deal flow suggests buyers are increasingly pursuing larger, conventional acquisitions aimed at securing technology, customers, data assets, and distribution.
SpaceX’s USD 54.75bn acquisition of Anysphere, the developer of AI coding agent Cursor, in June; Nvidia’s USD 12.93bn purchase of AI model repository Hugging Face in September; and AMD’s USD 8.2bn acquisition of spatial AI developer World Labs, also last month, all involved the purchase of established AI businesses.
That trio of deals marked a shift from the unprecedented capital raises by frontier AI models that defined the earlier wave of AI transactions. AI funding rounds were led by OpenAI’s USD 122bn raise in February 2026 and Anthropic’s USD 65bn in May, USD 30bn in February, and USD 15bn last November.
Alongside those mega financings came a succession of high-profile acquihire transactions, including Meta’s USD 14.3bn investment in ScaleAI, which brought founder Alexandr Wang onboard; and OpenAI’s USD 6.5bn acquisition of Jonny Ive’s IO Products, widely viewed as a talent and product-design driven transaction.
According to Mergermarket data, AI M&A and fundraising volume reached USD 450bn through the first nine months of 2026, triple the same period a year ago. Funding rounds accounted for 74% of that total. From June through September, however, traditional M&A accounted for 73% of total dollar volume.
While investors and advisors caution that AI remains an emerging industry and that buyers are still determining how to value AI businesses, they increasingly see acquisitions becoming an important complement to the funding rounds and acquihires that characterized the market’s earlier stages.
Three buckets
The growing prominence of large acquisitions suggests the AI market is in the early stages of maturing, said Ajay Agrawal, co-founder of Intrepid Growth Partners.
According to him, acquisitions now generally fall into three main categories.
In the first camp are purchases of novel algorithms and specialized talent, Agrawal said, pointing to AMD’s acquisition of World Labs. Founded by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, World Labs specializes in 3D ‘world models’ that are useful for robotics.
A second category includes acquisitions intended to gain access to customer bases and embedded workflow integrations.
The third type of acquisition involves strategics acquiring a “piece of the puzzle” for the creation of a broader end-to-end solution, Agrawal explained. Recent examples include Nvidia’s Hugging Face deal, as well as Salesforce’s roughly USD 2bn purchase of ListenLabs, which helps analyze customer interviews.
“People are starting to develop an intuition around what their full stack should look like,” he said.
Unlike previous technology cycles, AI improves through use, creating a feedback loop that strengthens products as they attract more users, Agrawal said. That dynamic is likely to accelerate AI dealmaking because companies may struggle to replicate years of accumulated learning once a rival establishes an early lead. That shifts the build-versus-buy calculus in favor of buying because time is more important than ever with AI.
“The more people that use it, the more it learns, and the better it continues to get. Because of that feature of AI, it’s really hard to catch up,” he said.
Despite the recent wave of large strategic deals, some believe the industry is still early in its ramp.
“It still feels like we are in the growth stage,” said Eric Issadore, a partner at Ropes & Gray. “I’m seeing a lot more of the minority investments, even if they’re not mega rounds, than traditional M&A.”
Mergermarket data supports that view: Funding rounds still account for about 60% of the total number of AI deals, a proportion that has remained constant over the last three years.
In other signs of a still-emerging industry, financial sponsors have yet to become major buyers of AI companies and acquirers continue to grapple with how to value AI businesses and their growth prospects, Issadore added.
But the emergence of those larger strategic acquisitions in recent months suggests the market is beginning a gradual maturation process, although it remains at an early stage, he said.From talent wars to applications
For Mark Kraynak, founding partner at Acrew Capital, dealmaking activity in AI is “all across the spectrum.”
“Way more than half” of Acrew’s portfolio companies are engaged in fundraising, acquisition discussions, acquihire conversations or broader strategic reviews, he said. “The market is very active.”
While hardware companies like Nvidia and AMD are making acquisitions to create ecosystems around AI, frontier AI labs are still frequently focused on talent.
“The labs are still incredibly acquisitive. I would say they are very hardcore about just buying talent,” he said.
But even among frontier model companies, priorities may be changing. As the capabilities of open-source models close the gap with the leading AI labs, questions are being raised over the long-term sustainability of their business models.
One concern is whether enough profit exists for infrastructure providers, foundation model developers, and application companies simultaneously. “Everybody needs margin in that picture,” Kraynak said.
Kraynak expects the leading model developers to want ownership of applications and customer relationships because those layers may provide stronger economics than foundation models alone. “They know there is likely more margin at the application layer,” he said.
Another source of future deal activity could come from the software sector. Issadore said many SaaS companies have spent the past two years figuring out how to incorporate AI into their products, either through internal development or acquisitions. Some that have succeeded and feel better insulated against the AI risk, may explore transactions or sale processes in the coming months.
If the first chapter of AI dealmaking was a race to fund the model builders, the next may be a race to own the businesses and applications that turn AI into enduring and profitable revenue streams.

data.title: Nemotron 3.5 Makes Nvidia’s Open A.I. Model Twice as Smart | Trending Topics
data.ai_summary: Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open model with 120 billion parameters, scoring 26 points on Artificial Analysis, twice its predecessor's 13. It also launched Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for laptops, scoring 21 points. The company plans to follow up with Bolt E4B for voice assistants.
data.author: Jakob Steinschaden; Co-Produced By Ai
data.full_text:
Nemotron 3.5 Makes Nvidia’s Open A.I. Model Twice as Smart
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Nvidia no longer just sells the shovels for the A.I. gold rush, it is now digging for itself: Last week, the chipmaker released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open model that, according to the benchmarking service Artificial Analysis, is twice as intelligent as its predecessor while producing about 60 percent less text. Nvidia also introduced Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a new family of models designed to run on laptops.
120 Billion Parameters and a One-Million-Token Context Window
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has 120 billion parameters, 12 billion of which are active per request. Besides text, the model processes images, web pages and PDFs, and Nvidia says it is especially good at reading tables, charts and scanned documents. Its context window holds one million tokens. It is built for corporate A.I. agents that work through multistep processes, operate software tools and review business documents.
Nvidia discloses more than many rivals: Along with the weights, released under the permissive OpenMDW-1.1 license, the company is publishing training data sets and recipes. The model was trained on about 26 trillion tokens and then post-trained with roughly 3.8 million examples and reinforcement learning. It is available on Hugging Face, through OpenRouter and as an Nvidia microservice. According to Artificial Analysis, API access costs about €0.21 ($0.23) per million input tokens and €0.51 ($0.57) per million output tokens.
Faster and Leaner Than Its Predecessor
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which combines 10 evaluations covering coding, agents, knowledge work and science, Super VL scores 26 points. Its predecessor, Nemotron 3 Super, scored 13, and Nvidia’s previous flagship, Nemotron 3 Ultra, scored 23. The new model generates an average of 46,000 output tokens per test task, compared with 114,000 for its predecessor.
Nvidia has also picked up speed. On a pre-release server run by the provider DeepInfra, Super VL reached about 630 tokens per second with very long inputs of 100,000 tokens. According to Artificial Analysis, that is the highest speed it has measured for any model scoring at least 20 points. The first word of a response arrives after 1.8 seconds. One reason is the 4-bit format NVFP4, which runs particularly efficiently on Nvidia chips. According to Artificial Analysis, it costs only 0.1 points of quality compared with the full weights.
Bolt: An Agent for Your Laptop
The second launch, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, is built to run locally. The first model in the family has 74 billion parameters, 9 billion of them active, and thanks to 2-bit quantization it fits into 24 gigabytes of memory. That means it runs on gaming PCs with RTX graphics cards, on Nvidia’s DGX Spark mini computer and on the new RTX Spark laptops, which went on sale last Friday. Popular tools such as Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp are supported.
Bolt scores 21 points on the Intelligence Index, just behind Nemotron 3 Ultra, which at 550 billion parameters is more than seven times its size. According to Artificial Analysis, it ranks fourth among models with fewer than 100 billion parameters and first among U.S. models in that class. The catch: Bolt is chattier, using 82,000 tokens per task, almost twice as many as Super VL. On Friday, Nvidia plans to follow up with Bolt E4B, a mini version for voice assistants and robots that needs just 4 gigabytes.
Who Already Uses Nemotron
Nvidia is deliberately positioning Nemotron as a foundation for other companies’ models. Salesforce has already built its reasoning model Koa on Nemotron, and Nvidia now lists partners including Atlassian, CrowdStrike, Perplexity, the chip design specialist Synopsys and the French software group Dassault Systèmes. Through Scale AI, Super VL was also post-trained for a due diligence agent at EY. How serious Nvidia is about its own models is also evident from its talks about acquiring the open-weight start-up Reflection AI.
A Lead With a Caveat
Artificial Analysis calls Super VL the best open model from the U.S. Close behind is Thinking Machines’ Inkling Small with 25.7 points. That title only applies to permissively licensed models, though: Meta’s Muse Spark Open, released the same day, scores 39 points on Artificial Analysis, but with 816 billion parameters it is much larger and comes with its own license that carries restrictions.
Internationally, the gap remains wide. The best open model from China, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, reaches 46 points, and K2 Horizon from the United Arab Emirates scores 31. Europe’s great hope, Mistral, scored 38 points on Artificial Analysis with Large 4. Nvidia is placing a different bet: Instead of building the smartest open model, it wants to deliver the fastest and cheapest one for agents that run around the clock. More details are likely on Wednesday, when Nvidia gives its keynote at GTC in Berlin.

data.title: Nemotron 3.5: Nvidia macht sein offenes KI-Modell doppelt so schlau | Trending Topics
data.ai_summary: Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open model with 120 billion parameters and a one-million-token context window. It scored 26 points in Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, double its predecessor's 13, and produces 46,000 output tokens per task versus 114,000. The company also unveiled Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for laptops.
data.author: Jakob Steinschaden; Co-Produced By Ai
data.full_text:
Nemotron 3.5: Nvidia macht sein offenes KI-Modell doppelt so schlau
Trending Topics auf Google als bevorzugte Nachrichtenquelle festlegen.
Nvidia verkauft nicht nur die Schaufeln für den KI-Goldrausch, der Chipkonzern gräbt inzwischen auch selbst: Mit Nemotron 3.5 Super VL hat Nvidia vergangene Woche ein offenes Modell veröffentlicht, das laut dem Testdienst Artificial Analysis doppelt so intelligent ist wie sein Vorgänger und dabei rund 60 Prozent weniger Text produziert. Dazu kommt mit Nemotron 3.5 Bolt eine neue Modellfamilie, die auf Laptops laufen soll.
120 Milliarden Parameter, eine Million Token Kontext
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL hat 120 Milliarden Parameter, von denen pro Anfrage 12 Milliarden aktiv sind. Das Modell verarbeitet neben Text auch Bilder, Webseiten und PDFs und ist laut Nvidia besonders gut darin, Tabellen, Diagramme und gescannte Dokumente auszulesen. Das Kontextfenster fasst eine Million Token. Gedacht ist es für KI-Agenten in Unternehmen, die mehrstufige Abläufe abarbeiten, Werkzeuge bedienen und Geschäftsdokumente prüfen.
Nvidia legt dabei mehr offen als viele Konkurrenten: Neben den Gewichten unter der freizügigen Lizenz OpenMDW-1.1 veröffentlicht der Konzern auch Trainingsdatensätze und Rezepte. Trainiert wurde das Modell mit rund 26 Billionen Token, nachtrainiert mit etwa 3,8 Millionen Beispielen und Reinforcement Learning. Erhältlich ist es auf Hugging Face, über OpenRouter und als Nvidia-Microservice. Laut Artificial Analysis kostet die Nutzung per API rund 0,21 Euro (0,23 Dollar) pro Million Input-Token und 0,51 Euro (0,57 Dollar) pro Million Output-Token.
Schneller und sparsamer als der Vorgänger
Im Intelligence Index von Artificial Analysis, der zehn Tests zu Programmieren, Agenten, Wissensarbeit und Naturwissenschaften bündelt, kommt Super VL auf 26 Punkte. Der Vorgänger Nemotron 3 Super lag bei 13 Punkten, Nvidias bisheriges Flaggschiff Nemotron 3 Ultra bei 23. Pro Testaufgabe erzeugt das neue Modell im Schnitt 46.000 Output-Token, der Vorgänger brauchte noch 114.000.
Auch beim Tempo legt Nvidia zu. Auf einem Vorab-Server des Anbieters DeepInfra erreichte Super VL bei sehr langen Eingaben von 100.000 Token rund 630 Token pro Sekunde, das ist laut Artificial Analysis der höchste gemessene Wert aller Modelle mit mindestens 20 Punkten. Das erste Wort der Antwort kommt nach 1,8 Sekunden. Möglich macht das unter anderem das 4-Bit-Format NVFP4, das auf Nvidias Chips besonders effizient läuft. Der Qualitätsverlust gegenüber den vollen Gewichten liegt laut Artificial Analysis bei nur 0,1 Punkten.
Bolt: Ein Agent für den Laptop
Die zweite Neuheit heißt Nemotron 3.5 Bolt und ist für den lokalen Einsatz gebaut. Das erste Modell der Familie hat 74 Milliarden Parameter, von denen 9 Milliarden aktiv sind, und passt dank 2-Bit-Quantisierung in 24 Gigabyte Speicher. Damit läuft es auf Gaming-PCs mit RTX-Grafikkarte, auf Nvidias Mini-Rechner DGX Spark und auf den neuen RTX-Spark-Laptops, die seit vergangenem Freitag erhältlich sind. Unterstützt werden gängige Werkzeuge wie Ollama, LM Studio und llama.cpp.
Bolt kommt im Intelligence Index auf 21 Punkte und liegt damit nur knapp hinter Nemotron 3 Ultra, das mit 550 Milliarden Parametern mehr als siebenmal so groß ist. Unter den Modellen mit weniger als 100 Milliarden Parametern ist es laut Artificial Analysis das viertbeste und das beste aus den USA. Der Haken: Bolt ist gesprächiger und braucht pro Aufgabe 82.000 Token, fast doppelt so viele wie Super VL. Am Freitag soll mit Bolt E4B noch eine Mini-Version für Sprachassistenten und Roboter folgen, die mit 4 Gigabyte auskommt.
Wer Nemotron bereits einsetzt
Nvidia baut Nemotron gezielt als Basis für die Modelle anderer Firmen auf. Salesforce hat sein Reasoning-Modell Koa bereits auf Nemotron aufgesetzt, nun nennt Nvidia unter anderem Atlassian, CrowdStrike, Perplexity, den Chipdesign-Spezialisten Synopsys und den französischen Softwarekonzern Dassault Systèmes als Partner. Über Scale AI wurde Super VL außerdem für einen Due-Diligence-Agenten von EY nachtrainiert. Wie ernst es Nvidia mit eigenen Modellen ist, zeigen auch die Gespräche über eine Übernahme des Open-Weight-Startups Reflection AI.
Spitze nur mit Einschränkung
Artificial Analysis bezeichnet Super VL als bestes offenes Modell aus den USA. Knapp dahinter liegt Inkling Small von Thinking Machines mit 25,7 Punkten. Die Krone gilt allerdings nur für Modelle mit freizügiger Lizenz: Metas Muse Spark Open, das am selben Tag erschien, kommt bei Artificial Analysis auf 39 Punkte, ist mit 816 Milliarden Parametern aber deutlich größer und steht unter einer eigenen Lizenz mit Einschränkungen.
International ist der Abstand ohnehin groß. Das beste offene Modell aus China, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, erreicht 46 Punkte, K2 Horizon aus den Vereinigten Arabischen Emiraten 31. Europas Hoffnungsträger Mistral kam mit Large 4 bei Artificial Analysis auf 38 Punkte. Nvidias Wette ist eine andere: Statt das klügste offene Modell zu bauen, will der Konzern das schnellste und billigste für Agenten liefern, die rund um die Uhr laufen. Mehr dazu dürfte es am Mittwoch geben, wenn Nvidia auf der GTC in Berlin seine Keynote hält.
Deals, Finanzierungsrunden und Tech-Trends, kuratiert von der Trending-Topics-Redaktion. Kostenlos seit 2015.

data.full_text:
New PayPal Gang: 10 Interns, 100 Billion Dollars

Core Viewpoint

Summary: How are Chinese Olympiad geniuses reshaping the AI and cryptocurrency world?

How are Chinese Olympiad geniuses reshaping the AI and cryptocurrency world?

Author: Xiaobing

On October 19, 2026, Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang posted a selfie on X with a caption of just seven words: got the HRT gang back together! The comments section exploded. This seemingly casual group photo hides one of the most outrageous facts in today's tech world: the three people in the photo, along with a few absent classmates, participated together in the inaugural internship program of Wall Street quantitative trading giant Hudson River Trading in the winter of 2015, which only recruited 10 people in total. Ten years later, the companies founded or led by these 10 interns have a combined valuation of over $100 billion. On the right side of the photo is Wang himself, 29 years old, founder of Scale AI, who was lured to Meta by Mark Zuckerberg for $14.3 billion last year to serve as Chief AI Officer, steering Meta's Super Intelligence Lab. On the left is Jeff Yan, founder of Hyperliquid, a decentralized exchange built by an 11-person team with zero funding, which made a profit of $900 million last year, with a project valuation reaching $76 billion. In the middle is Scott Wu, founder and CEO of Cognition, whose AI programming agent Devin is growing its enterprise customer base at a rate of 50% per month, with the company's latest valuation at $48 billion. The last time the three were in the same room together was probably still that winter of 2015, in the trading company's office by the Hudson River. Winter by the Hudson River The bond among these geniuses began in high school. Jeff Yan and Scott Wu both won gold medals at the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI), with Wu winning gold three times and topping the competition in 2014 with a perfect score. Alexandr Wang was a regular at the American Computer Olympiad and Math Olympiad, and they repeatedly met at various summer camps and training teams, in a circle small enough that almost everyone knew each other. In the winter of 2015, these competition prodigies scattered across Harvard and MIT were brought together by a common name: Hudson River Trading. HRT is one of the world's top quantitative trading firms, headquartered in New York, with a daily trading volume that once accounted for over 15% of the U.S. stock market. In the winter of 2015, HRT attempted to recruit interns for the first time. The spots were extremely limited, with only 10 available. Jeff Yan was a junior at Harvard at the time, Scott Wu was a freshman, and Alexandr Wang was a freshman at MIT. The design of this internship program was itself very "quantitative": lasting three weeks and conducted in a competition format, with rankings in each round. According to Jeff Yan's later recollection, the top two in every round were always him and Scott Wu. But perhaps the most historically significant moment of this internship was not the trading competition itself. According to an in-depth interview with Jeff Yan by Colossus magazine, it was during his internship at HRT that he first heard about Bitcoin through the recommendation of two former partners. Although he did not act on it immediately, he soon found the Ethereum white paper and read a description: a computer that runs globally and cannot be shut down, that seed grew into Hyperliquid years later. Also that winter, 19-year-old Alexandr Wang said something at his birthday party to his Harvard and MIT classmates that would be quoted repeatedly: "Why can't it be us?" Three Paths, One Origin After leaving HRT's office, these young people chose completely different tracks. But they share a common underlying logic: reconstructing a traditional industry with algorithmic thinking. Alexandr Wang: From Data Labeling to Zuckerberg's AI Brain After leaving HRT, Wang made a surprising decision: to drop out of MIT. In 2016, at the age of 19, he co-founded Scale AI with Lucy Guo, doing something that sounds anything but sexy: labeling training data for AI. But Wang's judgment was extremely precise: he skipped over specific AI applications and directly bet on the "shovels" of the entire AI industry. As the AI wave swept the globe, Scale AI became a core supplier for giants like OpenAI, Meta, and the U.S. Department of Defense. By 2021, the company's valuation soared to $7.3 billion, making 24-year-old Wang the youngest self-made billionaire in the world. In a 2024 funding round, Scale AI's valuation reached $13.8 billion, backed by Nvidia, Amazon, and Meta. Then came the deal in June 2025 that shook Silicon Valley. Meta acquired 49% of Scale AI for $14.3 billion, with an overall valuation of $29 billion. As a core condition of the deal, Zuckerberg required Wang to join Meta as Chief AI Officer, leading the newly established "Meta Super Intelligence Lab." A 28-year-old became the commander of the AI strategy for the world's largest social media empire. Jeff Yan: From Quant Trader to Builder of On-Chain Financial Infrastructure If Wang chose the "shovel business" of AI, Jeff Yan opted for the hardest path in the crypto world: rebuilding trading infrastructure. After graduating from Harvard, Yan did not rush to start a business. He worked at Google and a self-driving car company while continuously observing the crypto world. In 2020, he founded Chameleon Trading, a cryptocurrency market maker. This experience gave him a deep understanding of the structural flaws of centralized exchanges, and the collapse of FTX gave him a decisive push. In 2022, Yan disbanded the Chameleon team and began using his own funds to build Hyperliquid, a decentralized perpetual contract exchange running on the blockchain. No VC investment, no token presale, an 11-person team starting from scratch. This "anti-VC" path is almost unheard of in the crypto industry. Yan's confidence comes from the trading profits accumulated by Chameleon, and even more from the extreme pursuit of product quality by quantitative traders: low latency, high throughput, and user experience that approaches or even exceeds centralized exchanges. ICE's CEO Jeffrey Sprecher once stated that Hyperliquid's trading activity "surpassed that of Nasdaq." Today, Hyperliquid is one of the most profitable companies per capita in the world. Last year, the company's 11 employees generated over $900 million in profit. Founded just four years ago, its valuation has reached $76 billion. Scott Wu: The One Who Lets AI Write Code Scott Wu is the most formidable competitor among this group. Three IOI gold medals, crowned with a perfect score in 2014, a MathCounts national champion, and third place in Google Code Jam. After studying at Harvard for two years, he dropped out and co-founded the AI social networking platform Lunchclub. But what truly made him famous in Silicon Valley was the founding of Cognition at the end of 2023 with Steven Hao and Walden Yan (the three collectively hold 5 IOI gold medals). In March 2024, Cognition launched Devin, touted as the "world's first AI software engineer," capable of independently planning, writing, testing, and deploying code. Devin sparked significant controversy in the tech community, but the market provided its own answer: Cognition's valuation skyrocketed from $350 million in early 2024 to $10.2 billion in September 2025, and then to $26 billion in May 2026 (raising $1 billion), with annual revenue surging from $5.4 million in mid-2024 to nearly $500 million in mid-2026. By September 2026, annual revenue was approaching $1 billion, with the latest valuation reportedly reaching $48 billion. Wu himself stated that over 90% of Cognition's internal code is now written by Devin. A three-year-old startup, with a valuation increase from $350 million to $48 billion, rising more than 130 times. More Than Three People The selfie today features only three people, but this circle is much larger than a single photo can contain. According to Scott Wu, the HRT internship program was not the starting point of this group's friendship. Many of them had already met through various Olympiad competitions in high school. The names that extend from that small circle each occupy a place in today's tech landscape. Jesse Zhang, one of the HRT interns. His previous social gaming company Lowkey was acquired by Niantic (the developer of Pokémon Go). In 2023, he founded Decagon, an AI customer service agent company focused on replacing enterprise customer service with AI. The company has been established for less than three years and has reached a valuation of $4.5 billion, with clients including Duolingo and Hertz, and was selected for Forbes 30 Under 30 in 2026. Johnny Ho, a three-time IOI gold medalist and Harvard alumnus. He met Scott Wu and Jeff Yan in high school. In the group photo of the U.S. IOI team in 2013, he stood alongside Steven Hao and Scott Wu. After leaving the competition circle, Ho worked as a quantitative trader at Tower Research Capital and then joined Quora as an engineer. In 2022, he co-founded the AI search engine Perplexity with Aravind Srinivas and others, currently serving as co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer. Perplexity's latest funding round reportedly valued the company at about $30 billion, redefining the trillion-dollar search engine market. Demi Guo, a "genius girl" from Hangzhou, is a silver medalist at the 2015 IOI. She holds a bachelor's degree in mathematics and a master's degree in computer science from Harvard and was the youngest full-time researcher at Meta AI Research. In 2023, she dropped out of the Stanford PhD program and co-founded the AI video generation platform Pika with her classmate Chenlin Meng, which is valued at $470 million and has over 16 million users. She has interned at HRT and Quora, and is part of the same circle. Steven Hao, a gold medalist at the 2014 IOI, graduated from the MIT Department of Mathematics. He was an early core engineer during Alexandr Wang's time at Scale AI and later joined Scott Wu's Cognition as co-founder and CTO. According to Forbes estimates, 30-year-old Hao has a personal net worth of approximately $1.3 billion, making him the youngest American on the 2026 Forbes 400 list. Hao's trajectory clearly illustrates the "talent flow" within this circle: he brought the engineering experience and understanding of AI data he accumulated at Scale AI into Cognition. The three founders of Cognition, Wu, Hao, and Walden Yan, collectively hold 5 IOI gold medals, and they infused the algorithmic thinking honed in competitions directly into the core architecture of AI programming agents. Why Have Quantitative Trading Firms Become Cradles for Founders? This is not a coincidence. When Wang retweeted a group photo of interns from 2015 at the beginning of October this year, he added a comment: "HRT 2015 intern class is the new-gen PayPal Mafia." The story of the PayPal Mafia is well-known. Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, Reid Hoffman, David Sacks, and others emerged from the same company to create Tesla, Palantir, LinkedIn, Yammer, and other companies, defining the technological landscape of the last decade. However, there is a fundamental difference between this group from HRT and the PayPal Mafia. The bond among the PayPal Mafia is a company and a shared entrepreneurial experience. The bond among the HRT group is earlier and deeper; they share a way of thinking. What does it mean to come from a competitive background? It means they have been trained since their teenage years to solve problems with optimal solutions, possess an almost obsessive pursuit of efficiency, and have an intuitive understanding of complex systems. Quantitative trading firms are natural amplifiers of this way of thinking: at HRT, they learned how to extract signals from massive noise, make decisions within millisecond time windows, and build self-optimizing systems. Jesse Zhang wrote in an article: "The generation that grew up doing math, programming, and science competitions occupies a disproportionately high share among today's founders." Quantitative trading firms serve as a crucial springboard for this group transitioning from the competition circle to the entrepreneurial circle. Jane Street, Citadel, DE Shaw, Two Sigma—these names are backed by similar stories, but the concentration from the HRT class of 2015 is indeed exceptionally high. Out of 10 interns, at least 4 became unicorn founders, with a combined company valuation exceeding $100 billion. This "talent conversion rate" surpasses that of tech giants like Google and Meta, known for producing AI talent. The deeper reason may lie in the fact that these quantitative trading firms provide not only technical training but also an instinctive understanding of market structures. Wang applied this understanding to AI data infrastructure, Yan to on-chain financial infrastructure, Wu to software engineering automation, Zhang to customer service reconstruction, and Ho to search engine disruption. They solve different problems, but their approach to deconstructing problems is remarkably similar: find an inefficient system and rebuild it using algorithms and engineering capabilities. Geniuses always meet early. But what truly makes this story moving is not how smart they are. Competition gold medals have long proven their intelligence. What is moving is that the era has finally turned to the page that belongs to them. What was the image of this group ten years ago? Math competition champions, programming geeks, invisible people in social settings. In the hierarchy of any American high school, they were categorized under the same term: nerd. That term was not a compliment for a long time; it meant quirky, boring, and out of touch with the mainstream. But the world after 2024 has given nerds an unprecedented stage. As AI becomes the underlying operating system for all industries, and as code itself begins to write code, those who can master all of this are precisely those who have lived in algorithms and formulas since childhood. Wang, Yan, Wu, Zhang, Ho, Guo, Hao—these Chinese surnames that sound awkward when pronounced by white people have moved from the arena of competitions to the center stage of the era. The nerds who were once looked down upon have finally welcomed their golden age.

撰文：小饼

2026 年 10 月 19 日，Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang 在 X 上发了一张自拍，配文只有七个单词：got the HRT gang back together！ 评论区炸了。 这张看起来随意至极的合影，藏着当今科技世界最离谱的一个事实：照片里的三个人，加上他们不在场的几位老同学，在 2015 年冬天共同参加了华尔街量化交易巨头 Hudson River Trading 的首届实习生项目，那个项目一共只招了 10 个人。 十年后，这 10 个实习生创办或执掌的公司，合计估值超过 1000 亿美元。 照片右边是 Wang 本人，29 岁，Scale AI 创始人，去年被扎克伯格以 143 亿美元的代价挖去 Meta，出任首席 AI 官，掌舵 Meta 超级智能实验室。 左边是 Jeff Yan，Hyperliquid 创始人，一个零融资、11 人团队打造的去中心化交易所，去年利润 9 亿美元，项目市值高达 760 亿美元。 中间是 Scott Wu，Cognition 创始人兼 CEO，他的 AI 编程智能体 Devin 正在以每月 50%的速度增长企业客户，公司最新估值 480 亿美元。 三个人上一次同时出现在一个房间，可能还是 2015 年那个冬天，在哈德逊河边的交易公司办公室里。 哈德逊河畔的冬天 这群天才的缘分在高中时代就已经开始了。 Jeff Yan 和 Scott Wu 都在国际信息学奥林匹克竞赛（IOI）上拿过金牌，Wu 更是三次夺金，2014 年以满分登顶。Alexandr Wang 是美国计算机奥林匹克和数学奥林匹克的常客，他们在各种夏令营和集训队里反复碰面，那个圈子小到几乎所有人都互相认识。 2015 年冬天，这些散落在哈佛、MIT 各处的竞赛少年，被一个共同的名字聚到了一起：Hudson River Trading。 HRT 是全球最顶尖的量化交易公司之一，总部在纽约，日均交易量一度占到美国股市的 15%以上。 2015 年冬天，HRT 第一次尝试招收实习生。名额极少，总共只有 10 人。Jeff Yan 当时是哈佛大三学生，Scott Wu 是大一新生，Alexandr Wang 在 MIT 读大一。 这个实习项目的设计本身就很「量化」：为期三周，以竞赛形式进行，每一轮都会排名。据 Jeff Yan 后来回忆，每一轮的前两名，永远是他和 Scott Wu。 但这段实习最具历史意义的时刻，可能不是交易竞赛本身。据 Colossus 杂志对 Jeff Yan 的深度访谈，Yan 正是在 HRT 实习期间，从两位前合伙人的推介中第一次听说了比特币。虽然他当时并未立即行动，但很快就找到了以太坊的黄皮书，读到了一个描述：一台全世界共同运行、无人能关闭的计算机，那颗种子，在几年后长成了 Hyperliquid。 同样是在那个冬天，年仅 19 岁的 Alexandr Wang 在自己的生日聚会上，对围坐在桌旁的哈佛和 MIT 同学们说了一句话，后来被反复引用： 「为什么不能是我们？」 三条道路，一个原点 从 HRT 的办公室走出来之后，这些年轻人选择了完全不同的赛道。但他们身上有一个共同的底层逻辑：用算法思维重构一个传统行业。 Alexandr Wang：从数据标注到扎克伯格的 AI 大脑 离开 HRT 后，Wang 做了一个让所有人意外的决定：从 MIT 辍学。 2016 年，19 岁的他和 Lucy Guo 联合创立了 Scale AI，做的事情听起来一点都不性感，就是给 AI 训练数据做标注。但 Wang 的判断极其精准：他跳过了具体的 AI 应用，直接押注整个 AI 产业的「铲子」。 随着 AI 浪潮席卷全球，Scale AI 成了 OpenAI、Meta、美国国防部等巨头的核心供应商。2021 年，公司估值飙升至 73 亿美元，24 岁的 Wang 成了全球最年轻的白手起家亿万富翁。2024 年的融资中，Scale AI 估值达到 138 亿美元，背后站着英伟达、亚马逊和 Meta。 然后是 2025 年 6 月那笔震动硅谷的交易。Meta 以 143 亿美元收购了 Scale AI 49%的股权，整体估值 290 亿美元。作为交易的核心条件，扎克伯格要求 Wang 本人加入 Meta，出任首席 AI 官，领导新成立的「Meta 超级智能实验室」。 一个 28 岁的年轻人，成了全球最大社交媒体帝国 AI 战略的总指挥。 Jeff Yan：从量化交易员到链上金融基础设施的建造者 如果说 Wang 选择了 AI 的「铲子生意」，Jeff Yan 选择的则是加密世界里最硬核的那条路：重建交易基础设施。 Yan 在哈佛毕业后并没有急着创业。他先后在 Google 和一家自动驾驶公司工作，同时对加密世界的观察从未停止。2020 年，他创立了 Chameleon Trading，一家加密货币做市商。这段经历让他深刻理解了中心化交易所的结构性缺陷，FTX 的崩塌给了他决定性的一推。 2022 年，Yan 解散了 Chameleon 的团队，开始用自有资金搭建 Hyperliquid，一个运行在区块链上的去中心化永续合约交易所。没有 VC 投资，没有代币预售，11 个人的团队，从零开始。 这种「反 VC」的路径在加密行业几乎闻所未闻。Yan 的底气来自 Chameleon 积累的交易利润，更来自量化交易员对产品的极致追求：延迟要低，吞吐要高，用户体验要逼近甚至超越中心化交易所。 ICE 的 CEO Jeffrey Sprecher 曾称 Hyperliquid 的交易活跃度「超过了纳斯达克」。 如今，Hyperliquid 是全球人均盈利能力最高的企业之一。去年，这家公司仅有的 11 名员工创造了超过 9 亿美元的利润。公司成立仅四年，市值已达到 760 亿美元。 Scott Wu：让 AI 自己写代码的人 Scott Wu 是这群人里竞赛成绩最恐怖的一个。三枚 IOI 金牌，2014 年以满分夺冠，MathCounts 全美冠军，Google Code Jam 第三名。在哈佛读了两年书后辍学，与人联合创立了 AI 社交网络平台 Lunchclub。 但真正让他名震硅谷的，是 2023 年底与 Steven Hao、Walden Yan（三人合计持有 5 枚 IOI 金牌）联合创立的 Cognition。2024 年 3 月，Cognition 发布了 Devin，号称「全球第一个 AI 软件工程师」的产品，能够独立规划、编写、测试和部署代码。 Devin 引发了科技界的巨大争议，但市场给出了自己的回答：Cognition 的估值从 2024 年初的 3.5 亿美元一路飙升到 2025 年 9 月的 102 亿美元，再到 2026 年 5 月的 260 亿美元（融资 10 亿美元），年化收入从 2024 年年中的 540 万美元暴涨到 2026 年年中的近 5 亿美元。 到 2026 年 9 月，年化收入已逼近 10 亿美元，最新估值据报道已达 480 亿美元。Wu 本人说，Cognition 超过 90%的内部代码现在由 Devin 自己编写。 一个三岁的创业公司，估值从 3.5 亿到 480 亿，涨了 130 多倍。 不止三个人 今天那张自拍里只有三个人，但这个圈子远比一张照片能容纳的更大。 据 Scott Wu 本人补充，HRT 实习项目并不是这群人友谊的起点。早在高中时代，他们中的许多人就已经因为各种奥林匹克竞赛结识。而那个小圈子延伸出去的名字，每一个都在今天的科技版图上占据一席之地。 Jesse Zhang，同批 HRT 实习生之一。他此前创办的社交游戏公司 Lowkey 被 Niantic（《Pokémon Go》的开发商）收购。2023 年，他创立了 AI 客服智能体公司 Decagon，专注于用 AI 替代企业客户服务。公司成立不到三年，估值已达 45 亿美元，客户包括 Duolingo、赫兹租车等巨头，2026 年入选福布斯 30 Under 30。 Johnny Ho，三枚 IOI 金牌得主，哈佛校友。高中时就与 Scott Wu、Jeff Yan 相识。2013 年的美国 IOI 代表队合影中，他和 Steven Hao、Scott Wu 并肩站在一起。 离开竞赛圈后，Ho 在 Tower Research Capital 做量化交易员，随后加入 Quora 做工程师。2022 年，他与 Aravind Srinivas 等人联合创立了 AI 搜索引擎 Perplexity，目前担任联合创始人兼首席战略官。Perplexity 最新一轮融资的估值据报道已达约 300 亿美元，正在重新定义搜索引擎这个万亿级市场。 Demi Guo（郭文景），来自杭州的「天才少女」，2015 年 IOI 银牌得主。哈佛数学学士加计算机硕士，曾是 Meta AI Research 最年轻的全职研究员。2023 年，她从斯坦福博士项目辍学，与同学 Chenlin Meng 联合创立了 AI 视频生成平台 Pika，估值达到 4.7 亿美元，用户超过 1600 万。她曾在 HRT 和 Quora 实习，又是同一个圈子。 Steven Hao，2014 年 IOI 金牌得主，MIT 数学系毕业。他曾是 Alexandr Wang 在 Scale AI 时期的早期核心工程师，后来加入 Scott Wu 的 Cognition 担任联合创始人兼 CTO。根据福布斯的估算，30 岁的 Hao 个人净资产已达约 13 亿美元，是 2026 年福布斯 400 富豪榜上最年轻的美国人。 从 Hao 的轨迹可以清晰地看到这个圈子内部的「人才流动」：他把在 Scale AI 积累的工程经验和对 AI 数据的理解，带进了 Cognition。而 Cognition 三位创始人 Wu、Hao、Walden Yan 合计持有 5 枚 IOI 金牌，他们把竞赛中锤炼出的算法思维，直接灌注到了 AI 编程智能体的核心架构中。 量化交易公司为何成了创始人摇篮？ 这不是巧合。 当 Wang 在今年 10 月初转发那张 2015 年实习生合影时，他给它加了一句注释：「HRT 2015 intern class is the new-gen PayPal Mafia。」 PayPal 黑帮的故事人尽皆知。Elon Musk、Peter Thiel、Reid Hoffman、David Sacks 等人从同一家公司走出来，分别创建了 Tesla、Palantir、LinkedIn、Yammer 等公司，定义了上一个十年的科技格局。 但 HRT 这批人和 PayPal 黑帮有一个根本性的不同。PayPal 黑帮的纽带是一家公司和一段共同的创业经历。HRT 这群人的纽带更早、更深，他们共享的是一种思维方式。 竞赛选手出身意味着什么？ 意味着他们从十几岁起就被训练用最优解思维处理问题，对效率有近乎偏执的追求，对复杂系统有直觉性的理解。量化交易公司是这种思维方式的天然放大器：在 HRT，他们学会了如何在海量噪音中提取信号，如何在毫秒级的时间窗口内做出决策，如何搭建能够自我优化的系统。 Jesse Zhang 在一篇文章中写道：「做数学、编程和科学竞赛长大的这一代人，在今天的创始人中占了不成比例的高份额。」 量化交易公司正是这群人从竞赛圈到创业圈之间的关键跳板。Jane Street、Citadel、DE Shaw、Two Sigma，这些名字背后都站着类似的故事，但 HRT 2015 届的浓度，确实异常之高。 10 个实习生，至少 4 位成为独角兽创始人，公司合计估值超过千亿美元，这个「人才转化率」超过了 Google、Meta 等以盛产 AI 人才著称的科技巨头。 更深层的原因或许在于：这些量化交易公司提供的不仅是技术训练，还有一种对市场结构的本能理解。Wang 把这种理解用在了 AI 数据基础设施上，Yan 用在了链上金融基础设施上，Wu 用在了软件工程的自动化上，Zhang 用在了客户服务的重构上，Ho 用在了搜索引擎的颠覆上。 他们解决的问题不同，但拆解问题的方式如出一辙：找到一个低效的系统，用算法和工程能力重建它。 天才总是早早相遇。但这个故事真正动人的地方，不在于他们有多聪明。竞赛金牌早就证明了聪明。动人的地方在于时代终于翻到了属于他们的那一页。 十年前，这群人的画像是什么？数学竞赛冠军，编程极客，社交场上的隐形人。在任何一所美国高中的鄙视链里，他们都被归入同一个词：nerd。那个词在很长一段时间里不是褒义，它意味着古怪、无趣、与主流格格不入。 但 2024 年之后的世界，给了 nerd 们一个前所未有的舞台。 当 AI 成为所有产业的底层操作系统，当代码本身开始书写代码，能够驾驭这一切的人，恰恰是那些从小就活在算法和公式里的人。 Wang、Yan、Wu、Zhang、Ho、Guo、Hao，这些白人念起来拗口的华人姓氏，从奥赛赛场走向了时代的舞台中央。 曾经被鄙夷的 nerd，终于迎来了属于他们的黄金时代。

data.title: Meta’s ‘highest-paid employee’ Alexandr Wang on the WhatsApp message from Mark Zuckerberg that changed his career: Have time for a...
data.ai_summary: Meta's Alexandr Wang received a WhatsApp call from Mark Zuckerberg in April 2025, leading to a $14.3 billion investment and a 49% stake in Scale AI. Wang later sent a memo advising fewer, denser hires, and Meta released Muse Wonder in October 2025 as its first frontier-class model.
data.author: TOI Tech Desk
data.full_text:
In April 2025, Alexandr Wang was sitting in a staff meeting at Scale AI, the data-labelling company he co-founded, when his phone pinged. It was a
WhatsApp message from
Mark Zuckerberg: "Have time for a call?" Wang's first thought, as he tells it now, was simply, "huh, interesting."
That call ran for 44 minutes. Within two months, Meta had put $14.3 billion into Scale AI for a 49% stake and brought Wang in to run its AI efforts. Wang and Zuckerberg retold the story together on Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison, in an episode recorded around the release of Meta's new Muse Wonder AI model.
The timing of that message matters. Meta had released its Llama 4 models on April 4, 2025, to a lukewarm response. Around April 20, Zuckerberg said, he started calling people across the industry for advice on what to do next. Wang was one of them.
Alexandr Wang's memo told Zuckerberg to hire fewer, better people
Two days after the call, Wang sent Zuckerberg a long memo. Zuckerberg described it on Cheeky Pint as Wang laying out what he would do "if I were in your position."
The first point was about people, and how few of them Meta needed. "The very first thing is that you don't need a lot of people, and talent density is the thing that matters," Zuckerberg recalled.
That idea still shapes Meta Superintelligence Labs. Its core research team numbers under 200, "closer to 100," according to Wang, inside a company of roughly 75,000 employees.
The hire raised eyebrows. Wang, now 29, is an MIT dropout who built Scale AI into a key data supplier for the big AI labs, but he had never trained a frontier model. Collison pointed this out on the show. Zuckerberg said he spoke to the heads of research at all the major labs before deciding, and came away sure: "Alex is the guy."
What followed was a recruiting sprint Zuckerberg called "supernova." He cleared his calendar for a month or two just to meet researchers. "I don't think either of us slept that much for the first couple of months," he said.
Wang also recalled one early meeting that left him uneasy. When he said Meta's first priority should be a strong reasoning model, one of the existing leads asked whether consumers needed one at all. Wang said he called Nat Friedman, now head of Meta's AI products, straight after.
Meta's CFO warned Wang the AI bet had to work
By the end of 2025, the numbers had become enormous. Zuckerberg said Meta was preparing to "write this check for like, I don't know, like $100 billion, $200 billion" before anyone had seen the new models. "I'm like, Alex, are you sure this is going to work?"
At an executive gathering in Hawaii, Wang said, CFO Susan Li pulled him aside several times to drive the point home. "If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad." Wang admitted that all he had to show at the time was a "vibe report" on research progress and a few plots.
Muse and Muse Wonder have put Meta back in the AI race
The bet produced Muse Spark in April 2026, followed by the Muse personal agent app on September 8. Muse climbed to the top of Apple's App Store within days. Wang's own Muse, which he named Oiler, buys increasingly obscure teas from farms in Taiwan and Japan every week. Zuckerberg uses his to critique his MMA technique in the one-minute breaks between rounds.
On October 12, Meta released Muse Wonder, the first model it calls frontier-class. For now, it sits behind paid Muse subscriptions. Zuckerberg said the team was "very, very critical" of its own work along the way, and Wang describes the lab as a room full of "insecure overachievers."
Asked what kind of boss Zuckerberg is, Wang called him "very Bayesian," someone who updates his beliefs and then moves the whole company to match. A five-word WhatsApp message, and the 44-minute call that followed, is about as clear an example of that as Meta has.

data.title: Como um jovem de 28 anos conquistou Zuckerberg e virou peça-chave de uma aposta de US$ 130 bilhões
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang, 28, was recruited by Meta to lead its AI strategy, and the company plans $130-145 billion in capital investments for AI infrastructure. He now heads Meta Superintelligence Labs, developing the Muse models, with the first results announced in October.
data.author: Tamires Vitorio
data.full_text: RESUMO ＋ Alexandr Wang tinha 28 anos quando foi escolhido para comandar a nova estratégia de inteligência artificial da Meta. Cofundador da Scale AI, ele ajudou Zuckerberg a reorganizar a pesquisa da companhia e agora lidera o laboratório responsável pelos modelos Muse. Em abril de 2025, Alexandr Wang estava em uma reunião de trabalho quando recebeu uma mensagem de Mark Zuckerberg pelo WhatsApp. O fundador do Facebook queria conversar. A ligação durou cerca de 44 minutos e, dois dias depois, Wang enviou um memorando com o que faria se estivesse no lugar do empresário. Aos 28 anos, o cofundador da Scale AI começava a desenhar uma mudança que o colocaria no centro de uma aposta bilionária. Para este ano, a Meta prevê investimentos de capital entre US$ 130 bilhões e US$ 145 bilhões, destinados à infraestrutura que sustenta sua expansão — incluindo os sistemas de inteligência artificial que Wang agora precisa entregar. O episódio, reconstituído pelos dois no podcast Cheeky Pint, ajuda a explicar uma contratação que chamou a atenção pelo tamanho da responsabilidade entregue a alguém tão jovem. Hoje com 29 anos, Wang comanda o Meta Superintelligence Labs, laboratório criado para desenvolver os modelos mais avançados da companhia e transformar essa pesquisa em ferramentas usadas no cotidiano. A aproximação aconteceu quando Zuckerberg estava insatisfeito com o caminho seguido pela sua então família de IA Llama. Para Wang, a resposta passava por reunir uma equipe pequena, com profissionais excepcionais, e dar a ela condições de reconstruir o trabalho. A capacidade de recrutar essas pessoas pesou na escolha. “Alex é o cara”, disse Zuckerberg ao recordar sua decisão no podcast. Da Scale AI ao laboratório de Zuckerberg Nascido em Los Alamos, no Novo México, filho de imigrantes chineses, Wang aprendeu a programar ainda jovem e entrou no Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts, o MIT. Deixou a universidade aos 19 anos e, em 2016, fundou a Scale AI com Lucy Guo. A empresa cresceu fornecendo a outras companhias dados preparados para o treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial. Esse negócio o colocou perto de quem construía a tecnologia que agora precisa desenvolver. A Scale trabalhou com empresas de veículos autônomos, grandes grupos de tecnologia e clientes governamentais. Wang se tornou bilionário aos 24 anos, quando a startup alcançou uma avaliação de US$ 7,3 bilhões, em 2021. A mudança para a Meta veio acompanhada de uma operação de outra dimensão. Em 2025, a companhia pagou US$ 14,3 bilhões por uma participação de 49% na Scale AI. Wang deixou o comando executivo da startup para assumir o novo trabalho, mantendo um assento no conselho. O valor da transação não corresponde a uma remuneração pessoal de Wang. O acordo envolveu uma participação na empresa, recursos para o negócio e liquidez para acionistas. Ao anunciar a operação, a Scale afirmou que continuaria independente e nomeou Jason Droege como CEO interino. O desafio era montar uma equipe antes de entregar um modelo A escolha de Wang não seguiu o caminho mais óbvio de entregar o laboratório a um pesquisador conhecido por criar modelos de ponta. Ele ainda não havia comandado o treinamento de um desses sistemas. Zuckerberg apostou na experiência do empreendedor para reunir talentos, definir prioridades e mudar de direção quando os resultados exigissem. Segundo o relato publicado pela Fortune, o núcleo responsável pelos modelos tem menos de 200 pessoas, com um tamanho mais próximo de 100. Esse grupo depende de uma estrutura muito maior de engenharia, infraestrutura e desenvolvimento de produtos da Meta. A concentração de pesquisadores é parte da estratégia; os recursos necessários para sustentar o trabalho continuam espalhados pela companhia. No podcast, Zuckerberg recordou a incerteza de comprometer somas tão grandes antes de conhecer o resultado dos novos modelos. “Alex, você tem certeza de que isso vai funcionar?”, perguntou, ao recontar uma conversa daquele período. Muse coloca a aposta à prova Os resultados mais recentes dessa reorganização apareceram em 12 de outubro, com o anúncio do Muse Wonder e do Muse Wonder Full. Os modelos ampliam a família iniciada com o Muse Spark e foram apresentados pela Meta como ferramentas para agentes capazes de conduzir tarefas pessoais e profissionais. A empresa destaca recursos para recuperar informações de conversas anteriores, persistir em atividades com várias etapas e trabalhar com programação. O Muse Wonder foi disponibilizado pela Meta Model API e pelo Muse Code, enquanto a versão Full chegou aos assinantes do Muse Code. A integração ao aplicativo Muse foi anunciada para uma etapa posterior, começando pelos assinantes. É nessa passagem da pesquisa para o uso que a escolha de Wang será testada. A Meta quer que seus sistemas sejam capazes de receber uma tarefa, reunir as informações necessárias e executá-la com confiabilidade. Para o executivo que conquistou Zuckerberg com um memorando, o próximo desafio é fazer com que os produtos conquistem a mesma confiança de quem os utiliza. Perguntas frequentes Quem é Alexandr Wang? É o cofundador da Scale AI e chefe de inteligência artificial da Meta, onde lidera o Meta Superintelligence Labs. Alexandr Wang tem 28 anos? Ele tinha 28 anos quando foi recrutado pela Meta, em 2025. Atualmente, tem 29. Wang recebeu US$ 14,3 bilhões para trabalhar na Meta? Esse foi o valor da operação pela qual a Meta adquiriu 49% da Scale AI, não uma remuneração pessoal pelo cargo. O que é o Meta Superintelligence Labs? É o laboratório da Meta responsável pelo desenvolvimento de modelos avançados de inteligência artificial, incluindo a família Muse. Quanto a Meta pretende investir em 2026? A projeção apresentada no balanço do segundo trimestre é de US$ 130 bilhões a US$ 145 bilhões em investimentos de capital. O montante abrange a companhia, não apenas o laboratório de Wang.

data.title: QU, MCIT, Scale AI Collaborate On National AI-Powered Academic Advising Platform
data.ai_summary: Qatar University, MCIT, and Scale AI signed an agreement to build the National Co-Advisor Platform, an AI-powered academic advising tool. The platform will provide 24/7 student guidance and automate advisor tasks, with human oversight. It aims to support QU's Strategy 2023-2027 and Qatar National Vision 2030.

industries.name: Student Success, Advising & Case Management (Retention) Platforms

data.full_text:
QU, MCIT, Scale AI Collaborate On National AI-Powered Academic Advising Platform
Doha: Qatar University (QU), the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), and Scale AI have signed an agreement to collaborate on the development of the National Co-Advisor Platform, an AI-powered solution designed to enhance academic advising and support student success at QU.
The initiative is part of ongoing efforts to improve academic advising services through a unified digital platform that provides students and academic advisors with more efficient and flexible access to academic information and support, tailored to students' individual academic needs. The platform will combine an AI-powered interactive virtual assistant with advanced analytical tools that help advisors identify students who may require additional support, prepare for advising meetings, document outcomes, and follow up on required actions.
The platform will provide students with 24/7 access to personalized academic guidance, including information on academic program requirements, university policies and regulations, course registration eligibility and prerequisites, academic deadlines, and progress towards graduation. For advisors, it will automate a number of administrative and documentation tasks, allowing them to dedicate more time to personalized guidance, meaningful student engagement, and proactive support.
The initiative also seeks to strengthen early intervention by using academic data to identify indicators of academic difficulties and provide advisors with prioritized alerts and recommended interventions. In addition, the platform aims to reduce course registration errors that could affect student's academic progress or delay graduation. It will also provide university leadership with comprehensive insights and analytics to monitor academic progress and support data-driven decision-making.
The National Co-Advisor Platform will be integrated with QU's relevant databases, providing academic advisors with a comprehensive digital workspace and students with a round-the-clock virtual assistant, while ensuring human oversight of administrative processes and decisions.
Highlighting the importance of the collaboration, Dr. Shimaa Ali Al Quradaghi, Associate Vice President for Student Success and Development at QU's Student Affairs, said: "This partnership represents an important strategic step toward advancing academic advising at Qatar University and reflects our commitment to leveraging modern technologies and AI to enhance the student experience and promote academic success.
Through this platform, we aim to provide more personalized and proactive academic guidance, while enabling academic advisors to focus on direct, meaningful student engagement. This will help identify students' needs earlier, support informed academic decisions, and ultimately strengthen their journey toward successful degree completion.
Eman Al Kuwari, Director of Digital Innovation at MCIT said: "This collaboration reflects our focus on moving AI from potential to practical application by addressing real institutional needs. Through partnerships that bring together government, academia and technology providers, we aim to create an enabling environment for the responsible adoption of AI and the development of solutions that deliver measurable value. The National Co-Advisor Platform is a practical example of how AI can support more efficient and personalized services while maintaining human oversight as a core element of decision-making."
Amr Samir, Qatar Country Lead at Scale AI, said, "This agreement is the result of months spent listening to Qatar University's advisors, faculty and staff. Together with MCIT and Qatar University, we are building the National Co-Advisor Platform to put AI to work for students and the advisors who guide them, with human oversight at its core, in service of Qatar National Vision 2030."
The collaboration supports the objectives of QU's Strategy 2023-2027, particularly its focus on student centricity and digital transformation, while enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of academic support services. It also contributes to national priorities under the Third Qatar National Development Strategy by supporting the development of a highly skilled and productive workforce.

data.title: Novo CEO da Meta? Quem é Alexandr Wang, apontado como sucessor de Zuckerberg
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang, 29, is cited by the Financial Times as a possible successor to Mark Zuckerberg at Meta, though no CEO change has been announced. He leads AI and joined in June 2025 after a $14.3B Scale AI deal. The Muse Wonder model launch on October 12 boosted his position amid competition with OpenAI and Anthropic.
data.author: André Lopes
data.full_text: RESUMO ＋ Alexandr Wang, de 29 anos, é apontado pelo Financial Times como um possível sucessor de Mark Zuckerberg na Meta. Não há anúncio de troca de CEO: Wang comanda a área de inteligência artificial, enquanto Zuckerberg permanece à frente da companhia. O executivo chegou em junho de 2025, em meio à operação de US$ 14,3 bilhões envolvendo a Scale AI. O lançamento dos modelos Muse Wonder e Wonder Full, em 12 de outubro, deu novo impulso à aposta da empresa. A melhora dos produtos ainda convive com a disputa contra OpenAI e Anthropic. Alexandr Wang, de 29 anos, entrou no radar da sucessão de Mark Zuckerberg na Meta. Um perfil publicado pelo Financial Times apresenta o chefe de inteligência artificial da companhia como um possível futuro ocupante do cargo de CEO, após os lançamentos que deram novo fôlego à empresa na corrida pela tecnologia. A ascensão ganhou força com o lançamento do Muse Wonder, na segunda-feira, 12 de outubro. A apresentação impulsionou as ações da Meta e reforçou a posição de Wang, contratado em 2025 na esteira de uma operação de US$ 14,3 bilhões envolvendo a Scale AI, empresa que ele cofundou. Quem é Alexandr Wang Wang cresceu no Novo México, nos Estados Unidos, filho de dois físicos sino-americanos. Concluiu o ensino médio um ano antes do previsto, trabalhou no site de perguntas e respostas Quora e ingressou no Massachusetts Institute of Technology, o MIT, aos 18 anos. Deixou a universidade no ano seguinte para empreender. Em 2016, fundou a Scale com Lucy Guo. A empresa se especializou em preparar e organizar dados usados no treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, uma etapa da infraestrutura que atende aos desenvolvedores desses sistemas. A trajetória de Wang até a liderança de IA da Meta passou pela expansão desse negócio. A Scale anunciou a ida do executivo para a Meta em junho de 2025, junto de um investimento que avaliou a startup em mais de US$ 29 bilhões. O acordo manteve a empresa independente, com a Meta como acionista minoritária, e Wang permaneceu no conselho da Scale. Os US$ 14,3 bilhões correspondem à operação envolvendo a Scale AI, não ao salário de Wang. Por que Zuckerberg apostou nele Wang é visto como um executivo capaz de organizar equipes e conversar com engenheiros de IA. Sua contratação ocorreu durante uma reorganização da estratégia de inteligência artificial da Meta, após resultados que frustraram as expectativas em relação aos modelos da empresa. Segundo pessoas ouvidas pelo jornal, Wang e Zuckerberg discutiram a contratação em encontros ao longo de vários meses de 2025. O novo diretor recebeu amplo apoio do fundador e iniciou uma ofensiva para contratar pesquisadores de concorrentes. A aposta também trouxe pressão. De acordo com o FT, Wang chegou ao cargo sem ter trabalhado diretamente no treinamento de um modelo de IA, e os primeiros sistemas lançados sob sua liderança ficaram atrás dos rivais. Sua responsabilidade era transformar a contratação de talentos em produtos capazes de disputar esse mercado. O que mudou com o Muse Wonder A Meta apresentou Muse Wonder e Muse Wonder Full como seus modelos mais capazes até agora. Segundo a companhia, eles foram desenvolvidos para tarefas pessoais e profissionais que exigem várias etapas, como trabalhar com documentos e construir aplicativos. No anúncio de 12 de outubro, Wonder chegou à Meta Model API e ao Muse Code, enquanto Wonder Full foi disponibilizado aos assinantes do Muse Code. A empresa também anunciou que Wonder seria integrado ao agente pessoal Muse, começando pelos assinantes. A distinção ajuda a entender a aposta: Muse é o agente que usa ferramentas para trabalhar pelo usuário; Wonder é um dos modelos de IA que podem sustentar essas atividades. O avanço amplia a responsabilidade da equipe de Wang sobre produtos voltados tanto ao consumidor quanto aos desenvolvedores. Perguntas frequentes Qual é o cargo de Alexandr Wang na Meta? ＋ Wang é diretor de inteligência artificial, cargo conhecido como chief AI officer, e lidera o Meta Superintelligence Labs. Ele entrou na companhia em junho de 2025. Quantos anos tem Alexandr Wang? ＋ O executivo tem 29 anos. Antes de chegar à Meta, cofundou a Scale AI em 2016 e comandou a empresa. Wang recebeu US$ 14,3 bilhões de salário? ＋ Não. O valor se refere à operação envolvendo a Scale AI que acompanhou sua ida para a Meta, e não à remuneração pessoal do executivo. Qual é a diferença entre Muse e Muse Wonder? ＋ Muse é o agente pessoal da Meta, que pode usar ferramentas para executar tarefas. Muse Wonder é um modelo de inteligência artificial cuja integração ao agente foi anunciada pela companhia. Por que Wang é citado como possível sucessor de Zuckerberg? ＋ O Financial Times relaciona sua ascensão à liderança da área de IA e aos lançamentos recentes da Meta. A reportagem também descreve o apoio de Zuckerberg ao executivo, mas não apresenta um plano formal de sucessão.

data.title: A 44-minute call and a memo: How Alexandr Wang won Mark Zuckerberg’s trust—and a $100 billion-plus AI bet
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang was tapped to lead Meta Superintelligence Labs, and Muse, Meta's personal AI agent, launched in the U.S. on Sept. 8, topping 2.5 million downloads in two weeks. Meta expects 2026 capital expenditures of $130–145 billion, nearly double last year's $72.2 billion.
data.author: Emma Witman

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
Mark Zuckerberg once poured tens of billions of dollars into a metaverse that few people wanted to live in. Now he's spending even more on Muse, Meta's personal AI agent—the kind of assistant that, in Zuckerberg's case, coaches his MMA form between rounds and, in Alexandr Wang's, hunts down obscure loose-leaf teas from farms in Taiwan and Japan.
Those are a couple of the favorite use cases of Zuckerberg and Wang, the 29-year-old MIT dropout and Scale AI cofounder Zuckerberg tapped last year to lead Meta Superintelligence Labs. The Muse app launched in the U.S. on Sept. 8 and quickly became the most popular free app on Apple's App Store, topping 2.5 million downloads in about two weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN. On Monday, Meta followed up with Muse Wonder, the first model from the lab that Meta calls frontier-class.
"We're going to write this check for like, I don't know, like $100 billion or $200 billion," Zuckerberg said of discussions late last year, appearing alongside Wang on the latest episode of Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. "I'm like, Alex, you sure this is going to work?"

The Muse app launched in the U.S. on Sept. 8 and quickly became the most popular free app on Apple’s App Store, topping 2.5 million downloads in about two weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN. On Monday, Meta followed up with Muse Wonder, the first model from the lab that Meta calls frontier-class.

“We’re going to write this check for like, I don’t know, like $100 billion or $200 billion,” Zuckerberg said of discussions late last year, appearing alongside Wang on the latest episode of Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. “I’m like, Alex, you sure this is going to work?”
