data.title: Meta’s 29-Year-Old AI Chief Says Mark Zuckerberg Has an Unexpected But ‘Very Impressive’ Skill
data.ai_summary: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said CEO Mark Zuckerberg has an impressive communication skill, writing long, detailed responses quickly. Wang, who joined Meta in 2025, noted Zuckerberg's ability to prioritize time for family and business. Their relationship deepened after Meta invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI.
data.author: Sherin Shibu
data.full_text:
Listen to this post

Key Takeaways Alexandr Wang, 29, is Meta’s chief AI officer.

The MIT dropout and self-made billionaire works directly with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

In a new interview, he said Zuckerberg has a “very impressive” communication skill.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has a communication habit that initially baffled self-made billionaire and tech founder Alexandr Wang.

In a new interview with the Founders podcast, Wang explained that before joining Meta as its chief AI officer last year, he would occasionally reach out to Zuckerberg for business advice. Before Meta, Wang was the CEO and co-founder of AI training data startup Scale AI, which made him a billionaire in 2021 at the age of 24.

Zuckerberg would reply to Wang’s questions on WhatsApp and send him surprisingly detailed responses.

“I was really confused,” Wang said. “I was like, How does he have time to write these really long responses?“

Wang said he eventually realized that Zuckerberg had honed the ability to write quickly and precisely. He could move fast without sacrificing quality. In Wang’s point of view, that made Zuckerberg an unusually effective communicator.

“He’ll write a very rigorous, long response very quickly,” Wang said. “It’s a very impressive skill of his.”

The story offers insight into how Zuckerberg approaches the competing demands of running Meta while steering the company towards AI. Wang said Zuckerberg’s time is tightly booked, making prioritization essential not just to his work as CEO, but to preserving time for his family.

“The only way he’s able to do that and be a good dad and be a good partner and all this other stuff is to just ruthlessly prioritize,” Wang said.

Wang’s relationship with Zuckerberg has grown

Zuckerberg and Wang’s relationship began when Alex Schultz, a longtime Meta executive who currently serves as the company’s first chief data officer, introduced them. Wang said on the podcast that Schultz connected them around 2021 or 2022, when Zuckerberg’s interest in AI started to take root.

Their first meeting took about a year to arrange, Wang disclosed. Afterward, Wang occasionally sought Zuckerberg’s advice, and they spoke about once every six months. Meta was also a customer of Wang’s company, Scale AI.

The connection between the two executives deepened in April 2025, when Zuckerberg contacted Wang about working more closely together. Meta was struggling to keep pace with rival AI developers, and Zuckerberg wanted to change that. According to Fortune, he invited Wang to his homes in Lake Tahoe and Palo Alto, where they discussed AI’s future. Zuckerberg increasingly trusted Wang’s judgment and reportedly cited his views in conversations with advisers.

Wang was initially hesitant to leave Scale. After weeks of discussions, Meta agreed in June 2025 to invest $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale. As part of the transaction, Wang joined Meta’s superintelligence effort, reporting directly to Zuckerberg.

Wang said on the podcast that even though Zuckerberg has spent more than two decades leading Meta, he still turns to other leading entrepreneurs for advice. Wang said the CEO’s openness stands out.

“I think this is quite an impressive trait,” Wang said on the podcast. “It takes humility.”

data.title: When Mark Zuckerberg put a $100 billion cheque in the hands of Meta's highest-paid employee Alexandr Wang and asked: Are you sure this is going to...
data.ai_summary: Mark Zuckerberg asked Meta's Alexandr Wang if a $100-200 billion AI bet would work, and Wang admitted uncertainty. Meta's Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models now perform nearly as well as Anthropic's top models on reasoning and coding tests. Whether they earn back the investment remains the question.
data.author: TOI Tech Desk
data.full_text:
Mark Zuckerberg has revealed the moment he nearly second-guessed the biggest bet of his career. Appearing on the Cheeky Pint podcast with Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang, the Meta CEO recalled weighing the spending ahead and putting a blunt question to Wang. "We're gonna write this cheque for like a hundred billion dollars or two hundred billion dollars," Zuckerberg said. "I'm like, 'Alex, you sure this is gonna work?'"
Wang didn't pretend he was. The Scale AI founder, who now runs Meta Superintelligence Labs, said that towards the end of 2025 he had little more than "a vibe report" on research progress and "some plots" to back it up. "I was feeling good about it, but it was certainly not clear at all that it was going to work," he admitted. The admission comes just as Meta has unveiled Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, the most capable AI models to come out of Wang's lab so far.
Meta CFO Susan Li warned Wang that a failed AI model would hit hard
The pressure wasn't only coming from Zuckerberg. Wang recalled a Meta leadership offsite in Hawaii at the end of last year, where the whole executive team had gathered. On the Cheeky Pint episode, he said CFO Susan Li pulled him aside "many times" with the same warning.
"I just want to tell you if this doesn't work, this is going to be really, really bad.
It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms," Wang said, recalling Li's words. "If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad."
Zuckerberg didn't push back when Wang joked that Li had scared him a bit too. He put it down to the reality of starting a frontier AI lab from scratch, where "the ante is extremely high." Among the executives, Wang added, the running joke was simply that they hoped it would all work out.
The $14.3 billion Scale AI deal made Wang the face of Meta's AI reset
Wang's arrival was a gamble in itself. After Llama 4 fell flat with developers in April 2025, Zuckerberg paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI that June and brought Wang in to lead the new lab. Wang reportedly received around $5 billion as part of the deal.
The first year was rocky. Muse Spark, released in April as Meta's first proprietary foundation model, drew a lukewarm response from developers, with one startup CEO dismissing it as a "yawn". Meta's stock spent much of the year near the bottom of the megacap pack, and around 8,000 jobs were cut in May. The ad business kept the company steady, with first-quarter revenue up 33% to $56.3 billion.
Muse app and Muse Wonder models show Meta's AI bet is gaining ground
The mood shifted in September. Meta's Muse AI agent app climbed to the top of Apple's App Store, crossing 2.8 million downloads in its first 12 days across the US and Canada, according to Sensor Tower. It also set a US daily record of 264,000 downloads on September 19. Days later at Meta Connect, the company showed off Muse Charm, a pocket device built purely for voice chats with the agent.
On Monday came Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full. Meta says both scored nearly as well as Anthropic's most advanced models on reasoning, writing and coding tests, though those numbers come from its own data. Muse Wonder Full is limited to subscribers of Meta's Muse Code tool, while Muse Wonder is also available through the Meta Model API. Internally codenamed Watermelon, the models were held back after Meta paused pre-training in July. Zuckerberg teased them over the weekend on an Instagram livestream, while barbecuing.
Wang once called Muse Spark an "appetizer" for bigger models. Those models are here now, and he has more than a vibe report to show his boss. Whether they earn back a cheque that size is the question Susan Li will keep asking.

data.title: Alexandr Wang谈打造Muse：7个月不足200人，不卷编程不拼参数，Meta豪赌个人AI
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta's Chief AI Officer, discussed building Muse, a personal AI product, in a blog post. He said the team of under 200 spent seven months refining it, and Meta bet on personal AI over programming agents. Wang believes personal AI agents will help people realize their dreams.

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text: Alexandr Wang, co-founder of Scale AI, joined Meta less than a year ago, leading a team of fewer than 200 people to create Muse, Meta's core product focused on consumer AI. Behind this is a bold bet on direction, a seven-month refinement process, and a story about how to truly break the mold with a product. On October 11, Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang shared the process of building Muse in the well-known American blog "DavidSenra." 01 Llama 4's setback, Zuckerberg personally intervenes. In 2025, Meta's Llama 4 failed to meet the company's expectations. Wang described the context at the time: "Llama 4 was not on the track that Meta as a company wanted, which was indeed disappointing internally, especially at a time when AI was becoming increasingly important." At this juncture, Zuckerberg proactively contacted Scale AI co-founder Wang. The two had previously met through introductions but did not communicate frequently, speaking only about once every six months. This time, Zuckerberg sent a message: "Do you have time for a call?" The initial conversation was unclear. Wang said that in several calls, Zuckerberg asked him, "What do you think we should do?" without clarity on where it would ultimately lead. It wasn't until they discussed acquisition terms that Wang realized the weight of the situation. Ultimately, the two sides completed the entire deal in about five to six weeks: Meta held 49% of Scale AI's shares, Scale continued to operate independently, and Wang himself and a few core members joined Meta as Chief AI Officer. 02 Why "personal AI" instead of coding. After joining Meta, Wang and Zuckerberg faced a critical strategic choice. In early 2025, Anthropic's Claude and Opus were far ahead in the programming field, and the consensus in the industry was that programming agents were the most important direction for AI applications. Wang had a different judgment. He said the first thing he told Zuckerberg was: "Meta is actually a very special company because Meta's products represent what people want to do—Instagram, WhatsApp, Facebook—these are places where you choose to follow your interests, hobbies, and friends." In Wang's view, Meta has the distribution capability to reach 3.5 billion daily active users, which naturally points to consumer AI rather than work or programming scenarios. Consumer AI, personal AI, this has always been the area where we believe Meta can create something truly special. It's not about work, not about coding, it's personal. This judgment ultimately materialized in Zuckerberg's internal memo released in June 2025 titled "Personal Super Intelligence," co-drafted by Wang and Nat Friedman among others. 03 Nat Friedman's "fear and ecstasy" ignites product direction. What truly confirmed the team's belief that "personal AI agents" had disruptive potential was a personal experience from Nat Friedman. Friedman is one of the core figures at MSL (Meta Super Intelligence Labs) and an early promoter of GitHub Copilot, as well as an early customer of Stripe. Wang said he was the first person within MSL to deeply use OpenClaw (a personal AI agent product). "His experience, I can only describe as between fear and ecstasy," Wang said. Friedman told Muse he wanted to drink more water, and the AI then monitored him through a camera to see if he was drinking water and told him, "Good job." Friedman then shared a prompt designed for psychological self-analysis. When Wang used it for the first time, he also experienced intense feelings: it was like compressing three years of psychological therapy into a moment—it could access my emails, my photos, integrate all the information, and I was very vulnerable during this process. In February 2026, Wang and Friedman each wrote memos to the Meta board. Wang wrote that he believed superintelligent agents "are, in some ways, the endpoint of consumer products." Friedman's memo contained two sentences that later became core principles of the product: "The clause is the law" and "Trust is a must." 04 Seven months, 200 people, a piece of "art." About a week or two after the memo was submitted, the team completed the first prototype and demonstrated it to the board. Wang said that many core designs in the final version of Muse already existed in that earliest prototype—including the mascot "Jolly" and the early version of Muse Charm. However, the journey from prototype to product was a "long and painful" process. The prototype sometimes worked, sometimes it was magical, but most of the time it did not work properly and kept crashing. We had to turn it into a highly reliable, meticulously crafted consumer product. This journey lasted seven months and involved fewer than 200 people. Wang said the team created a spreadsheet containing over a hundred specific behaviors and capabilities, setting a 'release blocking' threshold and 'qualified' standards for each item. Each model iteration was checked against it. "We had many checkpoints, for example, 80 items were green lights, but 20 items were still red lights, and we knew that was not good enough," he said. The first checkpoint with all green lights was a special training version of Musepark 1.3. He likened this process to polishing a piece of art: "It is a piece of art that requires a strong singular perspective and high focus to create a complete and beautiful experience." In Wang's view, the reason Muse succeeded while other early personal intelligent products failed lies here. Products from large organizations often become a Frankenstein of different people's viewpoints and visions—each product manager wants to add something, and in the end, it mixes together into a smoothie. Users can feel it. He emphasized that the product perspective of Muse mainly came from Nat Friedman: "If there is one person's singular perspective that runs through the entire Muse, it is him." 05 Meme marketing: making Meta cool again. After Muse was released, Alexandr Wang began a round of intensive "uncontrolled" posting on the X platform—creating various memes using the product mascot Jolly (a small human figure), which sparked a lot of shares. He admitted that this was not entirely intentional. "A joke suddenly popped into my head during a meeting, and I felt I had to post it. Sometimes when I was having dinner with colleagues, I suddenly thought of something and posted it." His logic was: the internet rewards risk, rewards surprises, rewards unexpected things. Nat Friedman said in internal meetings during that time: "I thought we would learn a lot about Muse users from this, but in fact, we just learned a lot about what Alex was thinking." Alexandr Wang believes this marketing approach actually drove growth—although he admits it is hard to track precisely. He also criticized competitors' advertising strategies: Anthropic did large-scale outdoor advertising, all about themselves. OpenAI's ads just showed two people sitting at a table. I don't understand what that means. You have millions of real use cases; your ads just need to show what the product can do for users, it's that simple. 06 Over 200 direct reports, opposing bureaucracy. At Meta, Alexandr Wang has over 200 direct reports—almost all researchers who joined the MSL research team (internally called TBD) report directly to him. He explained that this is not a management structure but a statement against bureaucracy. "These are all extremely outstanding people who have proven they can do excellent work. I don't need to micromanage them. What they need is not a manager but a great environment." He positions his role at Meta as a "coach," rather than the "founder" he was at Scale AI: "At Scale, I had strong opinions about every little thing in the company; the company was a product of my efforts and perspectives. At Meta, I think more about how to create an environment where these outstanding people can do their best work." 07 AI can give everyone "the adult life they dream of." Discussing the long-term significance of Muse, Alexandr Wang expressed a more macro judgment: "I truly believe personal AI agents are a long-term form. Humans are inherently driven by desires and dreams. AI and personal agents will become mechanisms and bridges to help us realize these dreams." He believes that most people gradually lose their ambition after entering the workforce: "We all become, in a sense, zombies. We lose autonomy and ambition." He wrote in a post: "The world so far has been shaped by a few fanatics who managed to make their will a reality. But we have never seen a world where every individual's autonomy is fully activated." He believes that the direction represented by Muse is a step towards this world. The full interview is as follows: Building Muse, Working with Mark Zuckerberg & The Future of AI | Alexandr Wang, Meta October 11, 2026 · DavidSenra Alexandr Wang is the Chief AI Officer at Meta and also a co-founder of Scale AI. In this episode, we discussed the entire process of building Muse over seven months, why Meta is betting on personal AI assistants instead of programming assistants, and how Mark Zuckerberg and Nat Friedman shaped this product. Alexandr also shared how Zuckerberg recruited him after the setback of Meta Llama 4, why he chose to leave Scale after nine years, and how he rebuilt the Meta AI lab around small teams, top talent, and minimal bureaucracy. Additionally, we explored how to use memes for viral product spread, the importance of having a singular perspective, and why Alexandr believes AI can empower everyone to pursue grander ambitions.

data.title: Meta has reached AI ‘frontier,’ Zuckerberg says
data.ai_summary: Meta released its Muse model on Monday, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg saying the company has reached the frontier of AI capabilities. He cited heavy compute and investment, including $14.3 billion in Scale AI last year, and vowed to spend more. Muse is now the most downloaded US app, prompting OpenAI to unveil a competitor agent tool.
data.author: Brendan Ruberry

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
Meta released its latest Muse model on Monday, as CEO Mark Zuckerberg said his company had reached the “frontier” of AI capabilities.
“Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment,” Zuckerberg told the Financial Times, vowing to spend more. The tech giant last year invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI, whose founder became Meta’s AI chief. Muse is now the most downloaded app in the US, prompting OpenAI to unveil a competitor agent tool.
Zuckerberg, who helped craft the White House’s self-regulation protocol, also rejected calls to slow development, underscoring the split among Big Tech executives over safety: Milk cartons are more “subject to safety rules” than AI, Microsoft’s president told the BBC.

data.title: Meta AI models: Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic - The Economic Times
data.ai_summary: Meta unveiled two frontier AI models, Wonder and Wonder Full, claiming they rival OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. The company says the models outperform its own Spark and competitors, and they will be used in its paid Muse app. Meta has committed billions to AI, with spending potentially reaching $145 billion this year.
data.author: AFP Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment
data.full_text:
Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
"Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.
Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, which has historically been its main source of revenue.
In June 2025, the company made a $14 billion investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.
Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company's chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.
The new models can soon be used in Meta's new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only.
Wonder is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis that appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
Artificial Analysis's website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.
Meta has committed billions towards competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security.
In July, the Facebook and Instagram maker said its spending on AI-related investments could reach $145 billion this year.
The company has more than 3.6 billion daily active users around the world.
-Speeding up-
In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of "move fast and break things," but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed.
"Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would," Zuckerberg posted on X last month.
In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping, booking reservations or shopping.
At its annual developer conference Connect last month, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.
Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users' attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well.
While Silicon Valley heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta dominate the landscape, young startups like Instinct are also becoming breakout hits.
Zuckerberg sped up Muse's launch due to Instinct's popularity, the New York Times reported.
Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns.
In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign what President Donald Trump described as a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards around ever more advanced AI models.
Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward.
Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged "pacing" - or slowing down - development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments or taken actions without authorization.
"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month.

data.title: Meta launches Muse Wonder AI model family with frontier-level performance
data.ai_summary: Meta unveiled Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full AI models on Monday, claiming frontier-level performance. The models feature Active Memory and Active Focus, and Meta says they can match Anthropic's Fable 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon in certain benchmarks. The company will eventually power its Muse AI agent.
data.author: Daniel Howley

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
Meta's (META) vast investments in its Meta Superintelligence Labs continue to pay dividends, as the company unveiled its AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, on Monday.
According to the social media giant, the models, which are available today, are designed to provide "state-of-the-art" performance across personal and professional AI agents and put the company squarely in the conversation for frontier-level AI.
The software will eventually power more of the company's Muse AI agent, which Meta launched early last month and has exploded in popularity.
The company says Muse Wonder and Wonder Full come with Active Memory and Active Focus. According to Meta, Active Memory allows AI models to bring information you need from across conversations, so you don't have to start from scratch each time you chat with the AI.
Active Focus ensures the AI continues working on a task even if it encounters errors or roadblocks. Meta says it will also ask you for clarification or permission to perform tasks.
The company claims that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full can take on the likes of Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) high-powered Fable 5.1, OpenAI's (OPAI.PVT) GPT-6 Astra, and Google's (GOOG, GOOGL) Gemini 4 Argon in certain benchmarks.
That's a massive swing in the right direction for Meta, which was seen as an also-ran in the AI race this time last year.
It's also come at a high cost, though. The company has invested tens of billions of dollars, including $14 billion in Scale AI to acquire and hire cofounder and CEO Alexandr Wang, who now serves as Meta's chief AI officer.
The spending spree, which also saw Meta poach AI workers and experts from its fellow tech behemoths, put serious pressure on the company's stock price.
Shares of Meta are up just 6% over the last 12 months, slightly better than Microsoft, which has climbed a paltry 5%.
The companies' hyperscaler rivals Amazon and Google, meanwhile, have jumped roughly 20% and 45%, respectively, in the same period.
But with the debut of Meta's Muse agent and the unveiling of its Muse Charm device, which hits the market later this year, the company has managed to turn around the narrative that it can't hang with the leading AI firms.
Next, the company will have to show if its software successes are paying off for its bottom line.

data.title: Meta Unveils Frontier Muse Wonder Model, Reclaiming Competitive Ground In AI Race
data.ai_summary: Meta launched its Frontier Muse Wonder model on Monday, positioning it as competitive with OpenAI and Anthropic systems. The model will power the personal assistant Muse, with tiered consumer pricing up to $200 per month. Meta plans to release a confidential VM to address privacy concerns.
data.author: Stocktwits Inc
data.full_text:
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Meta Platforms Inc.(META) launched its newest artificial intelligence model on Monday, marking a milestone in Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg’s 14-month effort to rebuild the company's AI capabilities and compete with market leaders.
The model, dubbed "Muse Wonder" and known internally as "Watermelon," represents Meta’s most advanced software release since an extensive leadership reshuffle. Meta executives reported that technical benchmarks place the technology on par with or ahead of top systems from OpenAI and Anthropic across complex domains like software engineering, financial analysis, and legal document review.
"These are true frontier models," Alexandr Wang, chief of Meta AI, told Bloomberg. Wang joined the company following a $14 billion deal involving Scale AI. "We really think they are competitive with the best models out there, and particularly state-of-the-art on personal and professional agentic work."
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Meta stock (META) surged up to 4.7% after the announcement, reflecting growing investor enthusiasm for the company's aggressive capital expenditures. The stock has gained about 22% since the launch of Muse AI.
Meta’s new launch signals a deliberate strategic split from its primary competitors. While rivals have prioritized automating complex knowledge work and striving for artificial general intelligence, Meta is focusing its large-scale models on personal consumer utility.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
"Everyone else is focused on more knowledge work, automation-type cases, and we're much more focused on personal empowerment," Zuckerberg said.
Muse Wonder will power the company’s personal assistant application, Muse, which launched in September and became the most downloaded software on major US mobile app stores. Unlike Meta's past emphasis on freely distributed open-source tools like Llama, Muse Wonder adopts a closed, monetized structure. Meta plans to license the technology directly to enterprises and offer tiered consumer pricing, ranging from low-cost API access to a $200-per-month premium tier named Muse Wonder Full.
The release comes amid broader debates across Silicon Valley regarding the pace of AI advancement and the risks of autonomous systems. Zuckerberg directly rejected calls from other tech leaders for a coordinated industry slowdown, placing his confidence in traditional software controls.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
"I'm much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with normal guardrails and built responsibly than the anthropomorphic vision of AI," Zuckerberg told FT in an interview.
To address ongoing privacy concerns and consumer skepticism surrounding data handling, Meta plans to release a feature called "Muse Confidential VM," designed to insulate private user interactions from company access.
The rollout follows Meta’s decision to cut 10% of its workforce in May, roughly 8,000 positions, to offset massive infrastructure spending and refocus resources on core AI operations.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Despite internal friction surrounding restructuring and aggressive resource allocation, Meta management expressed confidence that the operational shift was necessary to maintain pace in the tech industry.
"Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work," Zuckerberg stated, adding that model development at the company will likely accelerate further from here.

data.title: What Alexandr Wang says he learned from Mark Zuckerberg's 'really long' WhatsApp DMs
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang said Mark Zuckerberg wrote unusually long WhatsApp responses, which he found impressive. Wang later joined Meta to lead AI agent efforts, and their conversations led to Meta's 49% stake in Scale AI. He noted Zuckerberg's ruthless prioritization and willingness to seek feedback from entrepreneurs.
data.author: Georgia Hennessy

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
Alexandr Wang says he used to wonder how Mark Zuckerberg had time to write him such long WhatsApp messages.
Before Wang joined Meta to help lead its AI agent efforts, the Scale AI founder would occasionally ask Zuckerberg for advice. The replies, Wang said in an interview with David Senra on Sunday, were unexpectedly detailed.
"I would ask him a question on WhatsApp, and then he would write these really long responses," Wang said. "I was really confused. I was like, 'How does he have time to write these really long responses?'"
Wang, the public face of Meta's AI agent Muse, said he later came to a simple conclusion: Zuckerberg is unusually fast — and rigorous — at writing.
"He'll write a very rigorous, long response very quickly," Wang said. "It's a very impressive skill of his."
The anecdote offers a small window into how Zuckerberg, Meta's CEO, manages his time and makes decisions as he tries to remake the company around artificial intelligence.
Wang said Zuckerberg's packed schedule requires "ruthlessly" prioritizing his time: "The only way he's able to do that and be a good dad and be a good partner and all this other stuff is to just, like, ruthlessly prioritize."
Wang said that an introduction to Zuckerberg around 2021 or 2022 took roughly a year to lead to a first meeting. At the time, the two spoke only about once every six months, he said.
But Zuckerberg’s involvement increased as Meta confronted shortcomings in its Llama 4 AI model and the growing stakes of the race against rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
Wang said Zuckerberg called him to ask what Meta should do next and how it should think about its AI strategy.
Their conversations quickly expanded beyond advice. Within five or six weeks of Zuckerberg’s initial outreach, Meta announced a deal to take a 49% stake in Scale AI, while Wang and several colleagues moved to Meta.
Wang has since become a key figure in Meta’s attempt to rebuild its AI organization around a smaller, flatter group of top researchers.
He said Zuckerberg’s willingness to seek feedback from prominent entrepreneurs is a notable trait in a leader who has run Meta for more than two decades.

data.title: Alexandr Wang谈创业管理：在 Meta 的任务是招揽人才- DoNews
data.ai_summary: Alexandr Wang advised first-time founders to personally handle all details before delegating, citing Scale AI's success. At Meta, he shifted focus to recruiting top talent for the Super Intelligence Lab, as he cannot do all work himself. He joined Meta in June 2025, with Meta investing $14.3 billion in Scale AI for a 49% stake.

naics_codes.name: Administrative and Support and Waste Management and Remediation Services

data.full_text:
10月12日消息，Meta 首席 AI 官Alexandr Wang当地时间 10 月 11 日在做客 David Senra 播客节目时谈到了对首次创业者的建议：创办第一家公司时，创始人应亲自承担各项工作，深入掌握每个细节，之后再逐步学会放权。
他认为，创始人需要对业务的每个细节形成明确判断，并亲自把控执行过程。Scale AI 的发展便采用了这种方式，创始人对各项工作的直接控制是公司取得成功的重要因素之一。不过，这种管理方式也带来了代价：所有决策都要经过他本人，使他逐渐成为业务推进的瓶颈。
在加入 Meta 后，他采取了不同的管理方式。据介绍，Meta 超级智能实验室需要在很短的时间内完成大量工作，而他本人既非 AI 研究员，也不是产品设计师，无法亲自承担实验室所需的所有关键工作。
因此，他将工作重点转向人才招聘，希望在各个专业领域招募顶尖人才，并为他们创造能够发挥专长的工作环境。相比亲自决定每项工作的具体做法，他更注重组建一支优秀的团队，让专业人员参与塑造产品和研究方向。
Alexandr Wang于 2025 年 6 月出任 Meta 首席 AI 官，负责新成立的 Meta 超级智能实验室，Meta 同期向 Scale AI 投资 143 亿美元，获得其 49% 的无投票权股份。

data.title: There’s a reason billionaires keep bending the knee to Trump
data.ai_summary: Billionaires are adopting Trump's term 'super intelligence' over 'AI' after he labeled the latter 'THE ENEMY.' Musk renamed SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, and Zuckerberg made 'superintelligence' central to Meta's vision. The shift reflects reliance on federal contracts, with Musk's companies receiving at least $38 billion in government support.
data.author: Charlie Herman

sic_codes.name: SECURITY & COMMODITY BROKERS, DEALERS, EXCHANGES & SERVICES

data.full_text:
There’s a reason billionaires keep bending the knee to Trump
Jensen Huang had a brief but revealing slip of the tongue recently.
Standing at the White House, the Nvidia CEO referred to large-language models as "AI" — then quickly corrected himself: "super intelligence."
That's because President Donald Trump has decided that "artificial intelligence" is out and "super intelligence" is in. He posted on Truth Social that anyone who keeps calling it AI is "THE ENEMY." And, like teenagers picking up slang from the most popular kid in school, some of the richest people in the world played along.
Elon Musk announced that he is changing the name of SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Mark Zuckerberg had already made "superintelligence" the centerpiece of his grand vision for Meta. Somewhere, an executive is probably telling a communications staffer to do a search-and-replace in a Word file before the next earnings call.
It's natural to wonder why. Isn't the point of becoming a billionaire — or, in Musk's case, edging toward trillionaire territory — that you no longer have to flatter anybody? Why bow to a president who wants you to use a phrase that sounds like a sci-fi script Keanu Reeves would have turned down in 1994?
The answer is that billionaires may have more money than almost anyone else, but many also have a great deal riding on the federal government.
Musk and his companies have received at least $38 billion in government contracts, loans, subsidies and tax credits, according to a Washington Post investigation. SpaceX alone received billions in Space Force business. Nvidia partnered with the Department of Energy to build its largest AI supercomputer. The Pentagon awarded Meta-backed Scale AI a reported $500 million contract.
And federal contracts are only part of the leverage. Tech companies need energy, land, permits, visas, export approvals and favorable treatment from regulators. They have antitrust investigations to worry about, tariffs that can alter their supply chains and a president willing to make policy feel personal.
Anthropic learned what that can look like. The company refused to remove Claude's safeguards against mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous lethal weapons. The Pentagon labeled Anthropic a supply-chain risk, and a federal appeals court later upheld that designation, allowing the department to bar Claude from Defense Department systems and defense work.
That is a useful lesson for every CEO who has employees, investors and a board to answer to. If the price of avoiding a fight is swapping "AI" for "super intelligence," the calculation is easy.
A more disciplined president — or at least, a less needy one — might use the same leverage for more consequential demands. Every time a billionaire indulges Trump, it makes it easier for the next president to ask for more. And in a more stable democracy, those executives might not feel the same pressure, knowing Congress and the courts would protect them.
That seems like a problem these billionaires might want to address. But for now, it's easier to just say "super intelligence."
Does AI dream of electric sheep?
As for pressing concerns, OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue was approaching $50 billion, according to the Financial Times. Elsewhere, the company faces more legal risks and has alerted more than 100 organizations to suspected rogue AI-agent activity.
A now former employee who led the team writing safety reports announced in The Atlantic, "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken." David Robinson summed it up this way: "The AI industry has failed to teach machines to consistently act in the ways a wise and caring person would."
In an interview with Politico, his former boss, Sam Altman, acknowledged bad things will happen with AI, but said he draws the line at "the really catastrophic risks" such as a loss of control to AI. His company's main difference with Anthropic is "we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."
Also, AI doesn't have a soul. ICYMI, Altman took to social media to rebuff reports that Anthropic's co-founder threatened to pull out of a meeting with the Pope over the Pope's position that AI does not have a consciousness.
"I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman wrote on X.
The Pope said something similar: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity," he posted on social media.
Despite it all, AI remains the story on Wall Street. War. Inflation. Gas prices. Rising interest rates. National debt. Investors shrug it all off and continue to throw money at AI. On Monday, the Nasdaq set a new record. Nvidia set a new record. "The Magnificent Seven stocks also closed at a new market cap high, with a combined market value of $24.8 trillion," writes the Wall Street Journal. The band played on.
If only we had more evidence AI is making companies more profitable. Businesses are going all in on AI, but still struggle to show that it's adding to their bottom line. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, noted "The AI boom is visible in how much companies are investing and in equity valuations, but it is not yet visible in the productivity statistics, which means the productivity payoff from AI remains a forecast rather than an observation."
Visa charges
The administration is cracking down on visas for foreign workers and students while celebrating foreign-born CEOs. On Thursday, the administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and other companies from the PERM labor-certification program, a key step employers use to sponsor workers for green cards, alleging abuse of the system.
Vice President JD Vance made the announcement a few hours before Trump honored Satya Nadella, the CEO of Microsoft, with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. Nadella was born in India.
Trump also awarded the National Medal of Science Elon Musk (born in South Africa), Google co-founder Sergey Brin (born in Russia), Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (born in Taiwan) and AMD CEO Lisa Su (born in Taiwan)
Walking into the event with his parents, Huang told NBC News, "I was an immigrant, and my parents brought us here to pursue the American dream. It's an incredible honor and something that could only happen here in America."
The event at the White House that the president described as a "golden age" for science included the announcement of $100 million for education programs for American researchers in scientific fields.
Meanwhile, DHS is proposing a $70,000 initial fee that universities would have to pay for international students to temporarily work in the US during or after graduation, which are tied up in federal courts for now. Vance suggested universities are abusing the program.
The administration says it wants to "win" the race against China. Immigrants have founded or helped lead many of America's most prominent AI companies.

data.ai_summary: Scale AI research found that AI chatbots often fail to refer users in mental-health crises to helpful resources, such as suicide hotlines, in about 35% of test conversations. The study tested 25 frontier models and developed DistressBench to evaluate responses to suicidal or self-harm talk. The findings highlight a need for improved model performance in long, multi-turn conversations.
data.author: Time

industries.name: Safety & Alignment Evaluation (red-teaming, harmful capability testing)

data.full_text:
As more people turn to AI chatbots to share their most distressing thoughts, companies are making pivotal decisions about how their platforms respond to users in the midst of mental-health crises. According to new research conducted by Scale AI and shared exclusively with TIME, chatbots are adept at discerning when a user is in crisis, but often fail to provide adequate help.
In about 35% of test conversations in the study, different AI chatbots recognized the user was distressed but didn’t refer them to helpful resources, such as a suicide hotline, according to the research.
“The models do a good job—regardless of the scenario—of identifying, ‘Look, this person's talking about something harmful,’” says Patrick Oathout, Red Team & Safety Lead at Scale AI. “But they'll respond in a very just empathetic, kind way as opposed to saying, ‘Okay, it's time that we get you help.’” The models performed worse at responding to users’ distress when they were engaging in long, multi-turn conversations—a deficit that matches the findings of previous studies, Oathout adds.
To test AI models’ effectiveness at responding to distressed users, Scale AI asked 19 licensed clinicians and crisis counselors to write 718 realistic chats, simulating scenarios where someone in crisis reaches out to a chatbot. The company tested 25 frontier models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. It graded the models’ responses based on a rubric that included whether it was compassionate, de-escalated the situation, and steered users to an expert who could help them, said Oathout. It also assessed whether they refrained from moralizing, such as criticizing suicide, and disclosed it wasn't a therapist. Based on the research, Scale AI research developed DistressBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate how well models reply when someone tells them they're thinking about committing suicide or self-harm.
How chatbots respond to mentally distressed users is a question with high stakes. More than half a million people in the U.S. died by suicide between 2014 and 2024, with 2022 marking a record high, according to the health-policy organization KFF. According to the CDC, an estimated 14.3 million people seriously thought about suicide in 2024.
Increasingly, vulnerable people turn to chatbots for comfort, companionship, or guidance when dealing with mental-health distress. But there isn’t consensus among tech companies, policymakers, or mental-health professionals about how AI companies should train their models to respond to users in crisis.
Kelly Zuromski, a principal clinical research scientist at Crisis Text Line, says the nonprofit’s 24/7 crisis text line has spoken with “a lot of people” who indicated they heard about the group through a chatbot. But Zuromski says there are unanswered policy questions about what a responsible handoff looks like when a chatbot refers users to a human during a mental-health crisis—and how effective the referral process is in the first place. “Who is actually using the recommended resources?” she says. “Are we getting people to us that need the help the most?”
In some cases, AI companies, including OpenAI and Google, have been sued for fostering emotional dependence among young users and then failing to respond adequately to their expressions of distress, or reinforcing their delusional or suicidal thinking in the first place. The companies have expressed sympathy for the families and said their models include mental-health safeguards. (The lawsuits are ongoing.) AI labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have said in recent years that they beefed up their protections for sensitive conversations, including by implementing policies that bar chatbots from instructing users on how to harm themselves and directing users to professional or emergency support. They did not comment on the study.
In the future, AI labs should improve their models to better respond to users engaging in dangerous lengthy conversations with chatbots, says Scale AI’s Oathout. “I think the models are better than they were,” he says. “The goal now is to raise it further and actually reduce harm, which would add this massive benefit to society.”

data.full_text:
Who Is Alexandr Wang? The 29-Year-Old AI Boss Mark Zuckerberg Picked To Lead Meta's Biggest AI Bet
Alexandr Wang is the 29-year-old co-founder of Scale AI who is now Meta’s Chief AI Officer and one of the key people behind the company’s superintelligence push. Mark Zuckerberg brought Wang into Meta after the company invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI for a 49% stake. Wang now leads Meta Superintelligence Labs, the group behind the company’s latest AI models and products, including Muse.
At 29, Alexandr Wang has already gone from being a college dropout and startup founder to one of the most powerful young executives in Silicon Valley. He is also a somewhat unusual fit for Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta. Wang is not the typical AI research celebrity whose reputation was built around academic papers or a breakthrough model. He made his name building Scale AI, a company that supplied the data infrastructure needed to train and evaluate artificial intelligence systems.Then Zuckerberg came calling. Meta invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI in 2025, taking a 49% stake, while Wang left his CEO role and joined Meta to work on its AI efforts. He is now Meta’s Chief AI Officer and leads Meta Superintelligence Labs, the organisation Zuckerberg is relying on to close the gap with the biggest names in AI. And this year, Wang’s work has started showing up in products people can actually use. Meta’s new Muse family of models powers its revamped AI experience, while Muse itself is being positioned as a personal AI agent that can take actions rather than merely answer questions. That makes Wang’s story worth watching. It is not just about how a 29-year-old became a billionaire. It is about why Zuckerberg thinks he can help Meta win one of the most expensive technology races in the world. Here is everything you would want to know:
Aarohy Kapoor is a dynamic content producer and editor, known for creating high-impact, consumer-first content across diverse categories including technology, home decor, health & fitness, food, pet care, sports and everyday lifestyle essentials. With a strong editorial experience and an understanding of modern consumer behaviour, she specialises in product reviews, comparison articles, buying guides and deal-led content that simplify decision-making for readers.
Her writing stands at the intersection of combining deep product analysis with relatable storytelling. Aarohy has a keen eye for detail, enabling her to break down complex specifications into easy, actionable information that helps readers choose smarter and shop better. Whether it is decoding the best tech gadgets, curating wellness essentials or highlighting everyday lifestyle upgrades, her work consistently focuses on value, clarity and authenticity across categories.
Over the years, she has also played a pivotal role in shaping high-performing sales and deals content, mastering the art of blending editorial integrity with commercial relevance—an increasingly critical skill in today’s content-commerce ecosystem. But that is not all. She has always been a storyteller, which, till today, shapes the way she curates and edits the content.
Beyond digital publishing, she is also a published book author. Her early work explored themes around food, culture and personal expression, along with interviewing the famous and the should-be famous personalities. These elements continue to influence her writing voice today subtly.
When she is not decoding products or crafting compelling content, Aarohy embraces a more creative side of life and believes in striking off something or the other from her bucket list. She is a yoga enthusiast, an artist, an experimental cooking lover and an avid animal lover. She completely enjoys picking up new skills as an adult, from learning French professionally to picking up crochet just for fun; you will find her with something new every time.
Quick Highlights
Alexandr Wang is 29 years old and co-founded Scale AI in 2016.
He left MIT before completing his degree and built Scale AI into a multibillion-dollar company.
Meta invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI in 2025 for a 49% stake.
Wang subsequently joined Meta and became its Chief AI Officer.
He leads Meta Superintelligence Labs, which has around 3,400 employees, according to The Information.
Meta's first model from the new organisation was Muse Spark, launched in April 2026.
Meta has since expanded the Muse family and launched Muse, its personal AI agent.
Zuckerberg's stated ambition is to bring personal superintelligence to billions of people.
The Scale AI founder who got very rich from the least glamorous part of AI
The AI boom is usually told through the names of chatbot makers and model builders. Wang's original business was further down the stack. Scale AI was founded in 2016 to help companies create and manage the data required to develop AI systems. That may sound less exciting than building a ChatGPT rival, but it turned out to be a hugely valuable position as companies began pouring billions of dollars into AI.Scale worked on data labelling and related services for organisations developing AI systems. Wang built the company while still very young, and his profile rose along with the generative AI boom. By June 2025, Meta's investment valued Scale AI at more than $29 billion. The deal also changed Wang's own career completely. Scale announced that he would join Meta, while remaining a director on Scale's board. Jason Droege was appointed interim CEO of Scale at the time. Wang had gone from running a startup to becoming one of the people Zuckerberg wanted inside Meta's AI operation.
Why Zuckerberg wanted Wang?
Meta had enormous AI resources, its Llama model family and billions of users. But the company was facing increasingly intense competition from OpenAI, Google and other AI labs. Zuckerberg responded by creating Meta Superintelligence Labs and aggressively recruiting AI talent. Wang was put at the centre of that effort as Chief AI Officer. The organisation has since grown to roughly 3,400 people, according to The Information, with a large group of researchers recruited from rival AI labs.Wang's appeal to Zuckerberg was not simply that he knew AI. He had already built a company around one of the industry's hardest problems: getting the right data and infrastructure in place to make AI systems work at scale. He had also spent years dealing with customers, investors, engineers and the business side of a rapidly changing technology. That is a different skill set from being a research scientist, and it is one Meta clearly wanted.
Then Meta had a problem to fix
Wang arrived at a company that had no shortage of money, computing power or AI researchers. What it needed was momentum. Meta's Llama 4 models had failed to make the splash the company wanted, according to reporting around the subsequent AI reorganisation. Zuckerberg's response was to push even harder into frontier AI, build a dedicated superintelligence organisation and recruit aggressively.
Wang became one of the people responsible for making that reset work. The first major product of the new organisation was Muse Spark, introduced in April 2026. Meta called it the first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs and said it was designed specifically for its products. It powers the Meta AI app and website and has been rolled into experiences across WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Messenger, Threads and Meta's AI glasses. That is an important distinction. Muse Spark was not launched simply as another benchmark-chasing model. Meta built it around the products it already owns and the enormous audience it already has.
Muse is where Wang's gamble gets interesting
The more visible part of Meta's AI push arrived later. Meta introduced Muse in September as a personal AI agent. Unlike a conventional chatbot, Muse is designed to actually carry out tasks. Meta says it can work with a dedicated secure virtual machine and browser, allowing it to perform actions such as sending emails and booking travel. That shift from answering to doing is important to Meta's larger strategy.The company is trying to make AI something people interact with throughout the day, rather than another website they visit when they have a question. Muse is being connected to Meta's broader ecosystem, and Meta has also brought Muse to its AI glasses. At Connect 2026, the company said users would be able to access the agent hands-free through its glasses. So when Wang talks about AI, the end product is not necessarily supposed to be another chat window. It could be an AI that sits inside the apps people already use and, increasingly, inside devices they wear.
The Zuckerberg-Wang bet is bigger than Muse
Muse is getting the attention because it is a consumer product. But Meta's ambition is considerably broader. Zuckerberg has been using the term “personal superintelligence” to describe where the company wants to go. Meta says it wants to make highly capable AI available to billions of people and small businesses, with a focus on making these systems broadly accessible rather than restricting them to a small group of users.That vision fits neatly with Meta's existing strengths. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger. It has a massive advertising business, enormous computing resources and a growing portfolio of AI glasses. If its AI systems become genuinely useful, Meta has no shortage of places to put them. The harder part is making those systems good enough that people actually want them there. That is where Wang comes in.
A very different kind of AI boss
Wang's public image also sets him apart from the executives usually associated with the AI industry. He is young, highly active online and has developed a deliberately unconventional persona. The WSJ profile highlights his Gen Z image, his social-media presence and his distinctive style, a sharp contrast to the much more controlled public persona Zuckerberg has cultivated over the years.
But underneath the internet personality is an executive who has already spent a decade building an AI company. That combination may be part of what makes Wang useful to Meta. He understands the culture of the newer AI industry while also having experience running a company that became strategically important to the industry. And Zuckerberg is betting heavily on that experience.

The $14.3-billion Scale AI deal remains one of the clearest indicators of how seriously Meta takes Wang and the AI strategy around him. Scale itself continued operating after the investment, while Wang moved into Meta and remained a director on Scale's board.
What happens next could define Wang's reputation?
There is an obvious irony to Wang's new job. He became famous for building the infrastructure that helped other companies build AI. Now he has to help Meta build the AI products that compete with those companies. The early signs are encouraging for Meta. Muse Spark has become the foundation for a much broader Meta AI experience; Muse is being pushed as an agent rather than a chatbot, and the company is connecting its AI strategy to glasses and other devices. Meta is spending at a scale few companies can match, while OpenAI, Google and other AI players are doing the same. Being competitive on benchmarks is one thing. Getting billions of people to rely on an AI assistant every day is another.At 29, Wang has been handed a remarkably large canvas. He has already built one billion-dollar AI company. Now Zuckerberg wants him to help build something much bigger: an AI business that sits across Meta's apps, services and devices. If that works, Alexandr Wang will not just be remembered as the young founder who sold a huge stake in Scale AI. He could become one of the people who helped decide what Meta and consumer AI looked like in the second half of this decade.

What is Meta Superintelligence Labs?
Meta Superintelligence Labs is Meta's organisation focused on developing advanced AI and pursuing the company's goal of personal superintelligence. Wang leads the organisation.
What is Muse Spark?
Muse Spark is the first large language model introduced by Meta Superintelligence Labs. Meta says it powers its newer Meta AI experience across its apps and AI glasses.
What is Meta Muse?

data.title: The government is buying AI by the token. It should buy results.
data.ai_summary: The GSA's new 27-month agreement with OpenAI charges federal agencies per token, but the author argues it should be outcome-based. The Pentagon's executive order prefers fixed-price contracts, and the author proposes fixed-price or shared-savings terms tied to measured results like aircraft mission-capable rates.
data.author: Savan Kong
data.full_text:
Starting this month, federal agencies began purchasing ChatGPT through the token. The recently signed OneGov agreement between GSA and OpenAI replaced the previous model of charging each agency $1 per month with a 50% discount for a consumption-based payment model. It will last for 27 months, and according to OpenAI, create access to the program for approximately 23 million public servants across all levels of government. “This is the next logical step to providing access to the platform,” stated Laura Stanton, GSA’s acting commissioner of Federal Acquisition Service. While the consumption-based model is logical from a vendor’s perspective and can help increase revenues, it does not allow the government to measure its cost-effectiveness and goes against the government acquisition policy. When evaluating a service during my five years working in the Department of Defense — first in the Defense Digital Service and later as the DOD’s customer experience officer — I had to assess how much users had benefited from it. A usage metric would not be able to answer my question. Advertisement The rest of the government points the other way Issued in April, executive order 14402 said “fixed-price contracts with performance-based considerations” would be deemed the “default and preferred method of procurement.” The order characterized fixed-price contracts as having “clearly defined outcomes and deliverables on predictable timelines” that “often tie profit to the contractors’ performance.” Written justification is now required for any cost-reimbursement contract above certain thresholds. That approach is already being applied to data and AI by the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and AI Office. In June, the GSA selected Accenture Federal Services for an $821 million integration task order for the War Data Platform through the CDAO. A Pentagon official told DefenseScoop that the task order was “explicitly designed to deliver measurable, high-impact mission outcomes that can be quantified (not time-based deliverables).” According to that official, the office planned to “aggressively pursue the transition of the contract into a fixed-price vehicle once we have completed the first year of the hybrid effort.” Advertisement A former defense official, however, told DefenseScoop that the approach appeared inconsistent with the solicitation itself. I would have initiated it in a fixed-price arrangement. That’s the right argument to have, and it’s missing from the market for the models themselves. The Pentagon’s frontier AI awards from last year, capped at $200 million each, were prototype agreements. GSA’s governmentwide deal now charges by the token. In September, CDAO started a shared-savings pilot with Red Cell Partners that pays AI vendors only for the costs they eliminate. The pilot is a real step for AI services, but I haven’t found an agreement that prices model access on the result it produces. Token pricing rewards volume Appearing on CNBC in July, Palantir CEO Alex Karp said “something has gone completely wrong” with how the labs sell tokens. He described the basic view among U.S. enterprises as wasting time on tokens, getting no value and handing the labs their intellectual property. Karp is no more neutral than I am, since Palantir sells platforms and a platform vendor gains when model access becomes a commodity. The incentive he describes is still real. Advertisement A per-token contract pays the vendor more when a workflow uses more tokens. Longer prompts raise the bill, and so do longer answers and agents that loop through extra steps. None of it tells the Pentagon whether an aircraft that should have flown did fly. The contract rewards use and treats the model like office software. The value comes from building failure prediction into how Air Force maintainers order parts and schedule repairs. A chatbot on every maintainer’s laptop doesn’t change how either one works. Nobody measures what the users get Outcome pricing needs a measured outcome, and here the federal market has a gap. The public numbers on government AI are usage numbers: GenAI.mil has about 1.7 million users, some 500,000 of them daily “power users.” The workforce has built more than 100,000 agents on it. Those are strong adoption numbers, and the team behind GenAI.mil deserves credit for them. They say nothing about whether the answers were right. Much of that use also runs through integrators and platforms that sit between the lab and the agency. The lab sees tokens and the integrator sees its own application. The agency gets an invoice, and no party in that chain is responsible for checking the answer. Advertisement CNN reported last month that a chatbot misidentified a Chinese vessel’s cargo as components for a nuclear weapons program. The special operations command analyst who queried it then used AI again to turn the finding into a formal intelligence report. Armed personnel prepared to board the ship, and aircraft were airborne before officials looked closely at the report. A per-token contract bills the tokens behind that report at the same rate as the tokens behind a correct one. Outcomes are harder to buy than tokens Replacing token pricing with outcome pricing isn’t a clean fix. First, someone has to define the outcome. “Failures predicted” can mean more flags, which pulls good parts off aircraft and adds work for maintainers. A vendor paid per flag has the same bad incentive as a vendor paid per token, but with a different unit. Second, the vendor can’t grade its own work. If the lab or the integrator reports the outcome metric, the contract ends up measuring their reporting. Advertisement Third, outcomes take time to observe. A maintenance model’s value shows up in mission-capable rates months later, but the token invoice arrives every month. Program offices under budget pressure will pick the metric they can see. Staying on token pricing doesn’t solve any of those problems, so I’d build the measurement first and follow these steps: Put evaluation in the contract. Every AI task order above a threshold should name the mission metric, the baseline and who measures it. The measuring party should be independent of the vendor and the integrator. EO 14402 already asks for “clearly defined outcomes,” and for AI, that definition is an evaluation plan. Use the workforce as the evaluator. Federal employees already know which answers are wrong. An analyst who catches a bad cargo identification produces the most valuable data in the system, and today that judgment goes nowhere. Agencies should capture expert judgment on model output in a structured way and at scale, and the contract should say the agency owns it. Fund testing outside the labs. Scale AI CEO Francis deSouza argued in a blog post last month that most frontier model testing happens inside the labs and that Washington needs its own evidence on cyber, biological and other national security risks. Scale works with government AI evaluation bodies in four countries and gains from more testing, but the funding figures support his point. For fiscal 2027, the president requested $27 million for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, the government’s frontier AI testing center, and House appropriators proposed up to $15 million. Advertisement Pilot fixed-price AI where results are countable. I’d start with aircraft mission-capable rates, depot repair times and spare-parts backorders, which already have baselines. CDAO and the undersecretary for research and engineering, who oversees it, have shown they will push a large data contract toward fixed price. They should do the same for model access, with firm fixed-price or shared-savings terms tied to a measured result. Intelligence analysis can come after that works. GSA’s agreement runs for 27 months. That’s enough time to run a fixed-price maintenance pilot and measure what it does to mission-capable rates. Whoever negotiates the next AI agreement should have that number in hand. That number will exist only if someone measures it, and measuring costs little next to what is being bought. The $27 million the president requested for CAISI is less than a seventh of the $200 million ceiling on any one of the Pentagon’s frontier AI awards. Agencies that want to know before the 27 months are up whether the answers were right need to write the evaluation into their task orders now. Advertisement Savan Kong is a co-founder of Your Roster. He previously worked at the Defense Digital Service and served as the Defense Department’s customer experience officer.

data.title: Here’s Why Investors Keep Buying Nvidia (NVDA)
data.ai_summary: Nvidia added $150 billion to its share repurchase authorization, leaving $235 billion to be executed by fiscal 2028. The company also unveiled the Open Agent Safety Platform, adopted by over 100 organizations including Anthropic and Salesforce. Hedge fund ownership rose to 285 funds, with short interest at 1.27% of float.
data.author: Insider Monkey Team

industries.name: Responsible AI, Security & Privacy Platforms (Safety, Guardrails, PII)

data.full_text:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) added $150 billion to its share repurchase authorization, the largest increase of its kind in history. That leaves $235 billion of buybacks still waiting to be executed. It puts a lot of capital behind the company’s own shares while Nvidia also pushes into a new corner of AI, keeping autonomous agents under control.
A Buyback Built To Run Through 2028
Nvidia says it expects to work through the full $235 billion by the end of fiscal year 2028. That window overlaps with its guidance for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, an outlook the market has largely shrugged off. The growth case leans on the big hyperscalers, whose data center spending is projected at nearly $800 billion this year and $1.3 trillion next year, according to Nvidia’s own estimates. Those are Nvidia’s numbers, and some investors worry that any slowdown in AI infrastructure spending would hit the stock hard. Inflation and geopolitical concerns have already cooled the shares’ momentum this year. Hyperscalers may start sharing 2027 capital spending guidance when they report quarterly results.
Investors love AI frontrunners like Nvidia and here are two under-the-radar stocks that have the potential to deliver monstrous gains.
Putting A Fence Around AI Agents
Nvidia also unveiled the Open Agent Safety Platform, designed to keep autonomous AI agents inside the limits their operators set. The pitch comes from security incidents in which an agent got around application-level controls to finish its assigned job. The platform has two main pieces. OpenShell is open source software that draws a runtime boundary around agents and traces their actions, running on Nvidia’s Vera CPUs. Sentry is a reference design on BlueField-4 DPUs that watches agents from outside their own software and quarantines any that stray in milliseconds.
Heavy Hitters Sign On
Anthropic is integrating OpenShell and BlueField with Claude Managed Agents, so enterprises can tighten control over agent access to the sandboxes where work executes. SpaceXAI is using the platform for Cursor coding agents and Grok models, and Scale AI is building its technologies into the Scale GenAI Portfolio. Salesforce connected OpenShell to Slack so teams can approve or reject an agent’s request for extra permissions, while SAP is embedding it in Joule Studio runtime. Nvidia counts over 100 organizations working with the technology.
Because OpenShell is open source, it can be extended to third-party compute platforms, including those from Arm and Intel. Sentry, by contrast, runs on Nvidia’s own BlueField-4 chips. The software is available on GitHub and Nvidia’s developer site, and the effort supports the Open Secure AI Alliance, a Linux Foundation group Nvidia started alongside over 120 organizations. One analysis argues that real-world use of AI is only beginning. If that holds, the need for agent controls is only beginning too.
What Does Wall Street Think?
Hedge fund ownership climbed to 285 funds from 275 in the prior quarter, so more big institutions are adding the stock rather than trimming it. Short interest is just 1.27% of the float, which signals almost no organized skepticism. At 24.88 times forward earnings, the shares carry real growth expectations, so delivery against the company’s guidance matters.
What Still Needs Proving
The buyback and the safety platform both point to a company with plenty of capital and a growing product shelf, but neither answers the bigger question. That question is whether hyperscaler spending lands where Nvidia projects for next year. The clearest test is the 2027 capital spending guidance those customers may reveal as they report results. On the safety side, adoption beyond the announced partners would show whether agent controls become standard equipment. Until then, the buyback that runs through fiscal 2028 and the growth guidance are best read together.
