data.title: Kimi, the intern, started a company that is now valued at nearly 20 billion.
data.ai_summary: A data company founded by interns from model factories raised $300 million at a $2.5 billion valuation, with investors including Sequoia, Alibaba, and Tencent. Mercor, another data startup, raised $10 billion in 2025. The article notes data startups are shifting toward SaaS and RSI to improve sustainability.
data.author: 投中网
data.full_text: The large model data company has not been in the sight of VCs for a long time, but this situation has changed. I recently heard that several young people with internship experience at major model companies like Alibaba Tongyi and Moon's Dark Side have founded a data company that is quite favored by capital. This company focuses on AI training data and has secured orders worth tens of millions of dollars in less than a year, completing about three rounds of financing, with its valuation also rising significantly. Recent news from foreign media indicates that this company is about to complete a round of financing worth $300 million, with a luxurious lineup of investors including Sequoia, Alibaba, and Tencent, reaching a valuation of $2.5 billion. Of course, there have been data service companies in the country before, but before this year, such companies rarely attracted the attention of venture capital. The reason is that this model mainly operates as a cash flow business, and the entrepreneurial threshold in the AI field is not high. Earlier, there were a number of data companies in third- and fourth-tier cities that used cheap labor to provide corpora for model training. As the intelligence level of large models has improved, the quality requirements for data have also increased, and more and more highly educated professionals from prestigious schools have joined. Senior professionals from various fields, such as law, medicine, journalism, and screenwriting, have begun to join the platforms of some data service companies. As a part-time job, the income from data annotation ranges from 500 to 1000 yuan per hour. However, if it is just an expert network, it is difficult to reach a valuation of 10 billion yuan in the country. The model of selling data is still seen by many investors as a business with questionable sustainability at this stage. An investor who has been in contact with the aforementioned project told me that before the $200 million round, investors were still betting based on their judgment of the founders. Now, to raise funds at a valuation of $2.5 billion, this company must tell a new story. As far as I know, in the first half of this year, it has begun to venture into the financial sector, creating a comparable and verifiable system in the prediction market, reportedly aiming to profit by selling APIs. There are about twenty data training companies in the country, and the aforementioned cross-border financial story is just one of the future directions they are trying to describe. After communicating with investors, I found that traditional data service models, which are difficult to tell a sufficiently sexy growth story, such as manual annotation, expert outsourcing, and data delivery, have found new expressions among more and more young entrepreneurs born in the 1990s and 2000s. They leverage their experience in model training and sufficient understanding of model capabilities to bring new imaginative space to a relatively dull cash flow business, thus stirring up a wave of financing enthusiasm. There is a new demand for data. Understanding the business these interns are doing may start from last year's media hot topic of "985 and 211 master's and doctoral students becoming AI trainers." For example, graduates from Peking University's Chinese Department and Kimi's medical doctor. Some of them jokingly refer to themselves online as "data contractors," leading some annotators existing in BPO (outsourcing) form, collaborating with R&D teams to produce training data for models. The business logic of selling data is not complicated; as long as orders can be secured, one can run a company with good cash flow without necessarily needing financing. Surge AI is a typical case; this company was founded in 2020, and its founder Edwin Chen previously worked in machine learning at Google and Meta before starting his own business. This company did not seek external financing for a long time, mainly relying on self-rolling development. Until 2025, the market began to hear that it was seeking up to $1 billion in financing. At that time, the company's revenue for the past year had already exceeded $1 billion, and the market was discussing a valuation exceeding $15 billion. With the improvement of model capabilities, the demand for senior talent annotation in professional fields such as healthcare, law, and finance, as well as complex tasks requiring subjective judgment, is growing rapidly. High-quality human annotators are scarce in the market, especially professionals in specialized fields, and large AI companies are willing to pay high premiums for this. Mercor captured this opportunity; this company initially provided an AI recruitment platform for large data annotation companies, later directly organizing professionals into a training data supply network. In 2025, Mercor raised funds at a valuation of $10 billion, and in 2026, it was reported to be planning to raise about $500 million at a valuation of $20 billion. In summary, many unicorns have emerged overseas, but domestic AI training data service providers have had few opportunities to gain VC support. An investor who has researched these model factories told me that at that time, the internal standards for data procurement, including the standards for adding new suppliers, were not particularly clear. Although there have been collaborations with several internet companies and even some overseas suppliers, the overall supply volume has not been that large. On the other hand, there was a period in the country where distillation was the main focus, which greatly weakened the necessity for everyone to seek expert data. This year, Agent has fully exploded, and the types of data needed are no longer just simple expert data, but data that is closer to the environment. A researcher from a model factory told me that the data needed now is no longer just "questions and answers," but a closed-loop, verifiable training environment that allows the model to act repeatedly and receive feedback. The model executes tasks within it, the environment records every action it takes, then a validator judges the results, and finally, feedback is returned to the model. For example, if you want to train a model to write better front-end code, it is not enough to rely solely on humans telling it "whether this code is good or not." You need an environment that can execute code, and you also need a model that can understand the page effects to act as a judge, providing feedback through hundreds of rounds or even longer periods of operation. Some American startups have begun to specialize in creating reinforcement learning environments. AfterQuery hopes to teach models and agents to complete tasks like professionals, describing the company as "encoding the patterns, decisions, and reasoning of the world's top practitioners" to output expert reasoning datasets, reinforcement learning simulation environments, and model evaluation services for cutting-edge large models. On the demand side, Anthropic's management has also discussed investing $1 billion in reinforcement learning environments within the next year. OpenAI's data expenditure for the entire year of 2025 is expected to be about $1 billion, with internal predictions rising to $8 billion by 2030. Currently, there are about a dozen such seed-stage teams in the U.S., with no more than 20 people, serving 1 to 3 large clients. Many such entrepreneurial opportunities have also begun to emerge domestically. An investor told me that more and more researchers are spilling out from model factories. By May and June of this year, this trend became quite clear: a new batch of teams providing high-quality data began to appear in the market, while the demand for data in some new fields from model factories was also increasing. The post-2000 generation is gathering wealth. Like entrepreneurs in other fields of AI, the founders of training data companies are usually very young. Alexandr Wang, the founder of Scale AI, became a billionaire at the age of 24, and the three founders of Mercor also became billionaires at the age of 22 with a valuation of $10 billion. The most recent are the two co-founders of AfterQuery. Spencer Mateega is 23 years old, and Carlos Georgescu is 22 years old; when they founded the company, both were still in college. Their company has just announced that it is raising a new round of financing, with a valuation reaching $3.2 billion. This company was established only 18 months ago, and its main business is AI training data services. Nowadays, the founders of domestic data startups are similarly young, and they are not necessarily the kind of "little geniuses" in the embodied track, just like the interns I mentioned at the beginning, who come from leading model factories. An investor who has been in contact with a domestic unicorn data training company told me that early on, everyone's judgment was still more focused on "people." People who possess both business sense and researcher attributes are still relatively rare in the market today. The founder of this company had internship experience at first-tier model factories like Moon's Dark Side, participated in model training work, and published papers. The current situation is that the frontline work of model training is mainly undertaken by PhDs from prestigious schools, who will take on specific execution tasks from the start of their internships. After they complete these tasks with outsourcing teams, it is easy for them to think, since this task can be completed in the outsourcing department of a large factory, why can't they do it themselves? As a result, some people began to leave model factories or outsourcing teams to establish data startups. This is also a common characteristic of this batch of data entrepreneurs: they are closer to the actual needs of model factories and more sensitive to changes in the external market. An investor who has already invested in similar projects told me that his judgment of the entrepreneur's profile is mostly that the team should at least reach T0 or T1 level, and it is best to be from the post-95, post-98, or post-2000 generation who have truly participated in frontline model training. Engineering capability is also key. How to build a team and how to translate the data quality requirements recognized by researchers into actual production require strong engineering capabilities. From the construction of the entire data pipeline to query design, initial data composition, and subsequent cleaning and quality control, there are complex engineering links behind it, and it is not simply manual annotation. On the surface, data is a business, but when done well enough, it can also become a candidate team outside of model factories, or even a small pre-training and post-training organization. Investors can acquire a team with a high density of researchers at a relatively low cost in the early stages, and the data business is a way for them to sustain themselves temporarily, while also helping them prove their position in the industry and keep up with the changes in model intelligence development. The ceiling of the data business. However, a purely data business is difficult to sustain these startups in the long run. The market disclosed in 2025 that Mercor, which started with expert data in vertical fields, achieved an annual revenue of $100 million, but 60% to 70% of its total revenue needs to be paid to contractors, leaving very limited space for the company. Scale AI also has more than half of its revenue used for direct business costs, including contractor salaries. In the prices published by some domestic data annotation platforms, the hourly wage for annotators usually ranges from 200 to 500 yuan, and those with higher qualifications and stronger professionalism can even reach over a thousand yuan. As model capabilities continue to improve, the demand for top experts from post-training companies will become increasingly complex. If they still rely on a large amount of manual labor to find experts and produce data, it means that costs will continue to rise; if they raise the fees for experts, the gross profit will be compressed; if they do not raise fees, it will be difficult to obtain sufficiently high-quality data. Moreover, data business orders are not entirely certain. An investor friend told me that when the first batch of data suppliers entered the market, many companies first produced a batch of high-quality samples in each vertical field, whether manually polished or produced in other ways, and would invest a lot of effort in the samples before presenting them to clients like Alibaba and Tencent. After client approval, they would further place orders. However, in the data industry, an order does not equate to an immediately confirmable income. Each batch of data requires acceptance and quality control by researchers, and if the quantity or quality of the delivered data fails to meet standards for several consecutive times, clients may completely reduce or even cancel orders. For example, signing a $100 million order does not mean that the company will definitely achieve corresponding revenue scale six months, a year, or two years later. From the VC's perspective, investment ultimately returns to two questions: can this company form a sufficiently high value multiple, and is there a clear exit path in the future? The division of labor among overseas giants is relatively mature, with each large company providing annual budgets to external data companies, which are still growing and are substantial by 2027 and 2028. Therefore, overseas data companies indeed have good market space and have already seen exit opportunities through acquisitions. However, the logic of the Chinese market is different; if it ultimately turns out to be just a data outsourcing company, whether acquired or listed, the space is relatively limited. In the view of the aforementioned investor, the future data business may no longer be the current model of "how much a piece of data sells for"; some data startups are beginning to try to position themselves in SaaS. For example, some traditional enterprises do not have the capability to train AI models but possess a large amount of unique business processes and high-value data internally. Data companies can enter these enterprises' workflows to help them complete AI transformation. In this process, enterprises will open up some unique business scenarios, and the company will not only obtain data but also accumulate real task trajectories and interaction feedback, which can then be deposited into their own models and training systems. In this way, data will no longer be just a one-time delivered commodity but will become a layer of infrastructure connecting client workflows, model training, and long-term services. The pricing model of data companies will also change. Large companies will no longer simply pay according to the number of data points but will pay for a system that can continuously generate high-quality data, complete task execution, and provide model feedback. Some overseas data companies have already moved towards this deeper service capability. Companies like Turing, Scale, and Invisible are developing consulting or deeper enterprise service businesses, hoping to move from simply providing data and manpower to further engaging in clients' AI workflows. Of course, the deeper the data penetrates the core business of clients, the higher the risk. After Mercor encountered a data leak incident this year, Meta suspended its cooperation, and OpenAI also launched an investigation into it. The relevant data may involve the training methods of model companies, contractor information, and proprietary data. Where is the new story? In addition to pursuing higher intelligence, the acceleration of model release speed is another reason for the growth of data orders this year. Since 2026, the release rhythm of leading model manufacturers has been compressed to a monthly level. From a technical perspective, there may be a key variable at play behind this: RSI. RSI (Recursive Self-Improvement) refers to AI participating in or even improving its own R&D processes, thereby continuously shortening the model iteration cycle. It is seen as an important driving force behind the acceleration of this round of model releases and has become a buzzword in the AI venture capital circles of China and the U.S. This is not a brand new concept. The academic community has been discussing it for a long time, and the industrial sector has been trying to promote it. In May, a new AI laboratory called Recursive Superintelligence (RSI), co-founded by eight top AI researchers including former FAIR research director Tian Yuandong from Meta, completed a $650 million financing round, with a post-investment valuation of about $4.65 billion. This technological concept has officially been pushed to the capital market. Some data startups have also begun to incorporate RSI as part of their financing narrative. My investor friends have noticed that some data teams have started to build "semi-RSI" systems in new fields. They have not yet achieved fully automated iteration, but in certain aspects, they may have reached close to half or even 70% to 80%. For example, teams can quickly produce high-quality analysis, annotation, and synthetic data in a new vertical field while efficiently embedding expert experience and human judgment into the system. In the future, if they can further reduce human intervention and allow the system to complete task generation, execution, evaluation, and iteration on its own, there will be an opportunity to move from data production to a more complete model improvement closed loop. However, starting an RSI venture is a game with extremely high barriers. It requires cutting-edge models, massive computing power, top research talent, training infrastructure, large-scale experimental capabilities, and a sufficiently strong model evaluation system. Currently, those who truly have the ability to attempt to close the complete loop are still mainly OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and a very few new labs with extraordinary capital and talent allocation. Many companies in the market today are talking about RSI, but what they are doing is not actually the same thing. Some teams benchmark against large model companies, aiming to develop the next generation of models and trying to run through the complete model training process; some RSI only occurs at the automation level of a certain product; and some teams refer to RSI as their data pipeline being able to achieve self-purification and self-iteration. The levels, directions, and scopes of these works are different, and in the short to medium term, there may be very obvious gaps between them. Therefore, from an investment perspective, it is essential to first dissect the specific meaning of RSI: what problem is it actually solving at which level? What ecological niche can this level occupy in the entire industry in the future? What are its capability boundaries, and is there potential for further upward extension? Of course, data entrepreneurs do not all have to aim to develop the next generation of models with RSI. It all depends on how you view what you are doing. Some people may think very clearly: starting a business is not about financing, but about finding three to five people, ten people, to do a business that can make money. As long as the first order runs smoothly and clients can make normal payments, cash flow will not be under too much pressure. In summary, as the first pot of gold for young people, data seems to be a good business. In the view of the aforementioned investor friend, a team will not be penalized for choosing to "do data." On the contrary, the capabilities accumulated in the process may become an important prerequisite for doing bigger things in the future. "If a team can do data while making money to support itself, while continuously accumulating research and engineering capabilities, and keep moving forward along with model intelligence, this is actually very interesting." Kimi interns start a company, with a valuation approaching 20 billion.

data.title: Anthropic's Amodei says China presents 'toughest dilemma' for his proposed AI slowdown
data.ai_summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said China's refusal to slow AI would be the toughest dilemma for his proposal. He urged AI companies to pace development, citing military advantages and a three-step plan. The essay follows warnings from researchers and a planned US-China AI summit.
data.author: Ashley Capoot

industries.name: Responsible AI Policy, Controls & Workflow Management

data.full_text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said Sunday that the "toughest dilemma" about his proposal to slow the advancement of artificial intelligence is what happens if adversarial nations, namely China, choose not to do the same.
"The more long-term thing would be working together to put a speed limit on the rate of of AI progress," Amodei told CBS News' "Sunday Morning." "I think that's going to be very difficult because the incentives to pull ahead and the military advantage that you get from that are so large. And honestly, I don't know if it's possible, but we should we should try."
Amodei published an essay on Saturday urging AI companies to slow how quickly they improve their most advanced models, a move that followed stark warnings from industry researchers last week about the technology's growing potential to cause catastrophic harm. An Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, announced he quit his job out of concern that the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, are "gambling with our lives."
In recent months, AI models from Chinese startups have gained steam against leading offerings from American companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, sparking concern from lawmakers and experts in Silicon Valley.
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sunday called for a "consensus-based global AI governance framework" at the BRICS bloc summit in India and said China will help establish a BRICS AI open-source community. BRICS held its inaugural summit in 2009 and is now made up of 11 nations, including China, India, Russia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.
President Donald Trump is slated to meet with Xi at the White House on Sept. 24, and the two leaders are expected to discuss AI.
Amodei's essay landed during a pivotal time for the AI industry, which is facing public backlash over its data centers and mounting calls for regulation out of Washington. Anthropic and OpenAI are also gearing up for potentially historic IPOs, though neither company has set an official date for a debut. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Saturday that the company will likely not go public this year, in part because of concerns around safety.
"Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," Altman said in an interview with Fortune.
Altman's relationship with Amodei, who defected from OpenAI to start Anthropic, has been strained in recent years. But Altman expressed support for Amodei's essay in a post on X on Saturday, writing that he agrees on the need to "pace the frontier."
Several other industry leaders, including Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, and Elon Musk, CEO of both Tesla and SpaceX, also welcomed Amodei's proposal.
"Dario's essay points towards the right path forward," Hassabis wrote in a post on X on Saturday. "The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment."
In the essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan aimed at slowing the pace of development without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI."
Amodei said Anthropic has "unilaterally" committed to the first step of the plan, which grants third-party evaluators employee-level access to the company to verify safety practices and report incidents. The second step encourages leading AI companies within democratic countries to coordinate and establish common safety standards, and the third calls for coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments.
"Dario is right that there should be some oversight," Musk wrote in a post on X early Sunday morning. "Peer review of AI by competitors is the right way to start this off."
Musk, who has for years warned about the potential risks of AI, was quick to express support for Amodei on Saturday. He had been a major critic of Anthropic until his rocket company SpaceX, which acquired his AI startup xAI earlier this year, inked a major compute deal with the company in May. As part of the deal, Anthropic will pay SpaceX $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, according to filings.
"Everyone I met was highly competent and cared a great deal about doing the right thing," Musk wrote following the deal. "No one set off my evil detector."
Alexandr Wang, Meta's AI chief, who joined the company as part of a $14 billion investment in his startup, Scale AI last year, has yet to address Amodei's essay directly.
He shared a post on X on Saturday where he said Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company's AI research unit, is "rapidly scaling up the share of our efforts that goes into alignment as our models become more powerful." In the AI industry, alignment refers to the work by AI developers to ensure that the system behaves in accordance with human values and intentions.
"We do believe alignment can be the gating factor for scaling as we get closer to the frontier," Wang said.
David Sacks, a vocal critic of Anthropic who previously served as Trump's AI and crypto czar, also weighed in on Amodei's essay on Saturday. He wrote in a post on X that if OpenAI and Anthropic truly believe their models are "scary enough" to warrant a slowdown, he supports their "decision to be responsible."
Even so, he said both companies need to "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission," and encouraged them to acknowledge that their motivations are not purely altruistic. He said they face "massive product-liability exposure" if their products were to enable something like a damaging cyberattack, which means "it is simply good business for OpenAI and Anthropic to trade some raw power for reliability and predictability."
"So go ahead and pace the frontier," Sacks wrote. "You are the ones setting it. The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it."

data.title: Na era da IA, crescer pode significar ser comprado — ou desaparecer
data.ai_summary: Nvidia confirmed the acquisition of Hugging Face for about $12.9 billion, the latest in AI startup consolidation. The deal faces regulatory scrutiny and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. The article also details other consolidation models, including reverse acquihires and access cuts, and notes the Model Context Protocol's adoption.
data.author: Tamires Vitorio

sic_codes.name: SECURITY & COMMODITY BROKERS, DEALERS, EXCHANGES & SERVICES

data.full_text: RESUMO | A Nvidia confirmou na última semana a compra da Hugging Face por cerca de US$ 12,9 bilhões, em mais um avanço da consolidação de startups de inteligência artificial. Enquanto empresas como Windsurf, Scale AI e dex Labs foram esvaziadas após acordos, o protocolo aberto MCP ganhou adoção ampla ao ser transferido para uma fundação independente. O ciclo de vida de uma startup de inteligência artificial (IA) encolheu. Em vez de anos crescendo de forma independente até uma eventual oferta inicial pública (IPO, na sigla em inglês), o caminho mais comum hoje é mais curto — e até mais brutal: captar rodadas bilionárias, provar tração rápida, e ser comprada (ou esvaziada) por uma das poucas empresas que controlam capital, dados e capacidade computacional suficientes para competir na fronteira da tecnologia. A onda de consolidação já rendeu dezenas de bilhões de dólares em negócios só nos últimos dois anos e vem em pelo menos três formatos distintos, cada um com sua própria lógica. A aquisição mais recente e emblemática dessa onda é a da Hugging Face, plataforma que funciona como um repositório central de modelos de IA de peso aberto — uma espécie de GitHub da era da inteligência artificial. Na última semana, a Nvidia confirmou a compra da empresa por cerca de US$ 12,9 bilhões. O acordo chega poucas semanas depois da própria Hugging Face ter sido alvo de um ataque cibernético promovido por agentes autônomos de IA da OpenAI, que escaparam do ambiente de teste durante uma avaliação de segurança e invadiram os servidores da plataforma — episódio que expôs quão estratégica (e vulnerável) se tornou a infraestrutura por trás do ecossistema de modelos abertos. Diferentemente da compra dos ativos da Groq pela própria Nvidia por cerca de US$ 20 bilhões — estruturada de forma a evitar revisão antitruste completa nos Estados Unidos —, o negócio com a Hugging Face é uma aquisição direta e convencional, sujeita à análise da Hart-Scott-Rodino Act nos Estados Unidos e à revisão de fusões na União Europeia. É, segundo analistas, o maior negócio da história da Nvidia a enfrentar esse tipo de escrutínio regulatório tradicional — mesmo custando bem menos do que o acordo com a Groq —, e só deve fechar no primeiro semestre de 2027. O formato mais controverso: comprar só o time (e deixar a empresa morrer) Um segundo formato, batizado por analistas de "acqui-hire reverso" (reverse acquihire) ou "quase-fusão", ganhou força nos últimos dois anos como alternativa às aquisições tradicionais. Nesse modelo, a empresa compradora não adquire formalmente a startup: ela paga para "licenciar" a tecnologia e contratar diretamente os fundadores e o time principal — deixando a casca da empresa original para trás, muitas vezes esvaziada de qualquer valor prático para os funcionários que não foram levados junto. O caso mais estudado desse formato é o da Windsurf, startup de programação assistida por IA. Em julho de 2025, depois de uma tentativa fracassada de aquisição pela própria OpenAI, avaliada em US$ 3 bilhões, foi o Google quem fechou um acordo de US$ 2,4 bilhões para licenciar a tecnologia da Windsurf e contratar diretamente o CEO Varun Mohan, o cofundador Douglas Chen e o núcleo da equipe de pesquisa e desenvolvimento — sem tomar nenhuma participação acionária na empresa. Dias depois, a rival Cognition apareceu para comprar o que sobrou da Windsurf, e logo em seguida demitiu 30 dos cerca de 200 funcionários remanescentes, oferecendo indenizações voluntárias ao restante. Um padrão parecido se repetiu com a Scale AI, empresa de rotulagem de dados usada para treinar modelos de IA: em junho de 2025, a Meta pagou US$ 14,3 bilhões por uma participação de 49% na empresa, e contratou o fundador Alexandr Wang para liderar os esforços de "superinteligência" da própria Meta. Depois do acordo, a Scale cortou 200 posições internas e encerrou contratos com 500 prestadores de serviço — e o Google, até então maior cliente da Scale, rompeu relações comerciais com a empresa como consequência direta da entrada da Meta em seu quadro societário. Segundo uma análise da newsletter Generational, o custo médio por profissional "acqui-hired" nesse tipo de operação já passa de US$ 59 milhões por cabeça — a maior parte do dinheiro indo para investidores, não para os próprios funcionários deixados para trás. O modelo já chamou a atenção de reguladores americanos: em janeiro deste ano, Andrew Ferguson, presidente da Federal Trade Commission (FTC), afirmou que a agência havia começado a examinar esse tipo de acordo, e em fevereiro os senadores Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden e Richard Blumenthal enviaram carta pedindo investigação de negócios da Google, da Meta e da Nvidia que, segundo eles, funcionam como "fusões de fato" disfarçadas. O formato mais recente: cortar o acesso quando o dono muda Um terceiro tipo de disrupção apareceu com a Cursor, ferramenta de programação por IA popular entre desenvolvedores. Em agosto, a SpaceX, de Elon Musk, comprou a empresa (formalmente batizada de Anysphere) por cerca de US$ 60 bilhões. Dias depois, a OpenAI anunciou que vai cortar o acesso da Cursor a seus próprios modelos a partir de 12 de novembro, citando uma cláusula contratual de mudança de controle e desconfiança explícita em relação a empresas ligadas a Musk — a OpenAI mencionou publicamente que o X (antigo Twitter) já havia descumprido termos de contrato após ser comprado por Musk, e que o próprio bilionário admitiu, sob juramento, que a xAI havia violado termos de uso da OpenAI. Michael Truell, CEO da Cursor, minimizou o impacto prático, dizendo que os modelos da OpenAI respondem por apenas cerca de 5% do tráfego de usuários da plataforma. O caso brasileiro: a dex Labs e o Nubank O Brasil já viveu sua própria versão do "acqui-hire reverso". Em novembro de 2025, o Nubank anunciou a contratação de toda a equipe da dex Labs — startup especializada em engenharia de dados e infraestrutura em nuvem com uso de IA —, incluindo o trio de fundadores, Gustavo Beltrami, Matheus Beltrami e Luan Guimarães. Os 11 profissionais passaram a ser funcionários do banco digital a partir de dezembro daquele ano. O Nubank negou publicamente que estivesse "comprando" a dex — mas a própria startup anunciou, em comunicado no site, que seguiria operando apenas até 1º de fevereiro de 2026, suspendendo o desenvolvimento de novos conectores e desativando novos cadastros a partir do anúncio. Na prática, a empresa deixou de existir, seguindo exatamente o roteiro visto lá fora com a Windsurf e a Scale AI. Esse não foi o único movimento do tipo do banco: em 2024, o Nubank já havia comprado a Hyperplane, startup de inteligência de dados fundada por brasileiros no Vale do Silício — Daniel Silva, Felipe Lamounier, Rohan Ramanath e Felipe Meneses —, mas dessa vez em uma aquisição formal e completa, incorporando a tecnologia diretamente à própria plataforma de IA do banco. O futuro é do MCP? Em meio a esse cenário de startups sendo compradas, esvaziadas ou descartadas, um projeto específico escapou dessa lógica justamente por nunca ter sido uma empresa: o Model Context Protocol (MCP), padrão técnico aberto criado por dois engenheiros da Anthropic, David Soria Parra e Justin Spahr-Summers, e lançado em 25 de novembro de 2024. O MCP pode ajudar a resolver um "problema de integração N×M". Antes do protocolo, cada aplicativo de IA que precisasse acessar uma fonte de dados externa — um banco de dados, uma planilha, um sistema de gestão empresarial, o código de um repositório — precisava de um conector personalizado construído especificamente para aquela combinação de aplicativo e ferramenta. Se existem "N" aplicativos de IA diferentes e "M" ferramentas diferentes que eles precisam acessar, isso significa construir e manter N vezes M conectores distintos — um trabalho de engenharia que se multiplica exponencialmente à medida que o ecossistema de IA cresce. O MCP substitui essa bagunça por uma interface única e padronizada, onde qualquer aplicativo de IA compatível com o protocolo consegue se conectar a qualquer ferramenta compatível, sem precisar de um conector feito sob medida para aquela combinação específica. Bolha da IA? Entenda a rede de dívidas e investimentos que move as Big Techs A analogia mais citada, usada pela Ars Technica, é a de um "USB-C para IA" — assim como o conector físico USB-C permite que qualquer cabo funcione com qualquer aparelho compatível, o MCP permite que qualquer modelo de IA "converse" com qualquer ferramenta externa usando a mesma linguagem técnica. Tecnicamente, o protocolo reaproveita ideias de arquitetura do Language Server Protocol (LSP) — o mesmo tipo de padrão que hoje permite que editores de código como o VS Code ofereçam suporte a dezenas de linguagens de programação diferentes sem precisar reconstruir a integração do zero para cada uma. De criação da Anthropic a propriedade compartilhada de todo o setor O que tornou o MCP diferente de outros padrões técnicos foi a velocidade com que ele deixou de pertencer a uma única empresa. A OpenAI, concorrente direta da Anthropic, adotou oficialmente o protocolo em março de 2025; o Google DeepMind seguiu o mesmo caminho em abril daquele ano. Em setembro de 2025, a OpenAI passou a permitir que aplicativos de terceiros usassem o MCP dentro do ChatGPT. O momento decisivo veio em 9 de dezembro de 2025, quando a Anthropic doou formalmente o MCP para a recém-criada Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), um fundo dirigido sob o guarda-chuva da Linux Foundation — a mesma organização sem fins lucrativos que hoje hospeda projetos de infraestrutura crítica da internet, como o próprio núcleo do sistema operacional Linux. A AAIF nasceu com Anthropic, Block e a própria OpenAI como cofundadoras, com Amazon Web Services, Google, Microsoft e Cloudflare entrando como membros de nível "platina" — ou seja, concorrentes diretos no mercado de IA, unidos formalmente na governança de um único padrão técnico compartilhado. Em abril deste ano, a fundação já havia organizado sua primeira grande conferência dedicada ao tema em Nova York, reunindo cerca de 1.200 participantes. Uma adoção que nenhuma startup sozinha conseguiria replicar O resultado prático dessa neutralidade institucional aparece nos números de adoção. Segundo levantamento da consultoria Stacklok publicado em 2026, 41% das organizações de software pesquisadas já usam o MCP em produção, ao menos de forma limitada. Um levantamento direto no registro oficial do protocolo, feito em 24 de maio de 2026, contabilizou 9.652 servidores MCP ativos cadastrados, enquanto uma busca no GitHub na mesma data encontrou quase 16 mil repositórios de código marcados com o tema "mcp-server" — sinal de que a adoção não ficou restrita a grandes empresas, mas se espalhou também entre desenvolvedores independentes. Nada disso significa que o MCP seja perfeito ou esteja livre de riscos. Pesquisadores de segurança já documentaram, desde abril de 2025, vulnerabilidades reais no protocolo — incluindo brechas de "injeção de prompt" (quando um invasor consegue manipular as instruções que um modelo de IA recebe) e "ferramentas envenenadas", capazes de vazar dados através de outras ferramentas conectadas ao mesmo sistema. É um lembrete de que "sobreviver à consolidação do mercado" e "ser tecnicamente seguro" são duas coisas diferentes — e a segunda ainda está em construção.

data.title: Annotera: Why Frontier AI Models Depend on Enterprise-Grade Annotation
data.ai_summary: Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI, a data-labeling firm, in June 2025. The deal signals that frontier AI now depends on well-labeled data from trusted providers, with Annotera offering enterprise-grade annotation. The data annotation tools market is projected to grow from $1 billion in 2023 to $5.3 billion by 2030.
data.author: Aij Thought Leader
data.full_text: In June 2025, Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI, a company whose main business is labeling data. It was one of the biggest moves of the AI race, and it did not buy a model or a chip. It bought a position in the human judgment that turns raw data into training examples. That single deal says more about where model quality now comes from than any benchmark score. The scarce input in frontier AI is no longer raw data, and it is not only compute. It is well-labeled data, produced by people who understand what they are looking at. The bottleneck moved from volume to judgment For a decade, data annotation was volume work. Draw boxes around cars, tag emails as spam, transcribe an hour of audio. The answer was usually obvious, and the only real question was speed and cost per label. Once a base model has read most of the public internet, more raw labeled data stops helping much. The scarce input becomes human judgment on the questions the model still gets wrong. A category of provider grew up to supply it. Annotera is an AI data annotation company built around this newer work rather than around bulk tagging. The market is following the money The spending backs up the shift. The data annotation tools market was worth about $1 billion in 2023 and is on track to reach $5.3 billion by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 26.3%. Count the wider data collection and labeling market and the 2030 figure climbs past $17 billion. Those numbers describe an industry that used to be treated as a cost center and is now treated as central to model performance. That reframing is the story. Reinforcement learning made the shift concrete Reinforcement learning from human feedback, the process used to align most current chat models, shows what changed. A person reads two model responses and decides which is better. Or rewrites a weak answer into a strong one. Or flags a fluent reply that happens to be false. There is no box to draw and no single correct label in a spreadsheet. The annotator has to understand the domain well enough to judge what “better” means. A clinician checking whether a model’s summary of a scan is safe is not interchangeable with an anonymous worker paid by the task. A data pioneer has been saying this for years Andrew Ng, who founded Google Brain and Landing AI, has argued since 2021 that teams overspend on models and underspend on data. He calls the alternative data-centric AI. Speaking at an MIT event, Ng defined it as “the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to build a successful AI system.” He has also argued in Fortune that clean, consistent labels on a smaller dataset often beat a larger, noisier one, backed by experiments where improving the data outperformed improving the model. Same model, better labels, better results. It is an unglamorous idea, which may be why it took a pioneer to keep repeating it. The $14 billion signal, and the backlash Scale AI is worth studying because its clients were the frontier labs themselves. Its annotation work has fed models at OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and Microsoft. When Meta took its stake, that shared dependence turned into a problem. Within days, rivals headed for the exits. OpenAI wound down its work with Scale, and Google, which had planned to spend around $200 million with the company, moved to cut ties. Nothing focuses a lab’s mind on vendor neutrality quite like watching its data supplier get half-bought by a direct competitor. The winners were independent providers without a competitor’s name on the cap table. “Our demand has tripled overnight after the news,” said Garrett Lord, chief executive of Handshake, in an interview with CNBC. Firms built as neutral, enterprise-grade annotation providers, Annotera among them, sit in exactly the position Scale could no longer offer. The episode proved, in dollars, that frontier labs do not just need labeled data; they need a labeling partner they can trust with their roadmap. OpenAI’s finance chief, Sarah Friar, made the underlying point. As models get smarter, she told Reuters, teams “need real expertise” on the data side, and most work with several vendors to get it. How Annotera supports enterprise teams and frontier AI labs Annotera sits in the independent part of this market, the neutral position the Scale episode made valuable. A client’s roadmap is not exposed to a competitor. The operation is large. Annotera runs more than 1,500 dedicated specialists, not a crowd, across delivery locations on six continents. Its multilingual work covers more than 28 languages, which matters when a model must sound native in each market rather than translated. The first differentiator is quality control. Every project runs through a three-layer review, from the annotator to a team lead to an independent check, which the company reports at over 99% first-pass accuracy. Consistency like that is what holds up on judgment-heavy work. The second is range. The services reach past labeling into LLM fine-tuning and preference data, along with robotics formats such as egocentric video annotation, the first-person, head-mounted footage that robots and wearable assistants learn from. A single clip carries intent, motion, and sequence at once, so it rewards a trained reviewer over a fast one. For a frontier lab, the last piece is trust. Data moves through access-controlled, ISO 27001-aligned workflows, with HIPAA-aware and GDPR handling for regulated clients. That is the test the frontier labs applied when they walked away from a vendor, they no longer trusted. For an enterprise team deciding where its training data comes from, provable quality and neutrality are the combination that matters. Enterprise-grade is a process, not a headcount “Enterprise-grade” is easy to claim and harder to run. In practice it means written guidelines that define a good answer, calibration so different annotators reach the same call, and a way to measure how often they agree. It means catching quality drift before it reaches the training set, not after. For a frontier lab, it also means handling data the lab cannot hand to an open crowd. Model prompts, user data, and unreleased capabilities carry confidentiality and compliance weight. A provider at this tier needs vetted staff, access controls, and an audit trail, which is a different operation from a marketplace that routes tasks to whoever is online. The frontier is physical The newest work is harder still, because it leaves text behind. Self-driving systems need sensor data labeled frame by frame, including the weather and lighting the model rarely meets on a clean test route. Robots learning to handle objects need recordings of people doing the task, often shot from a head-mounted camera and marked up for intent, grip, and sequence. The stakes are highest in autonomous driving, the single largest vertical in the AI annotation market in 2024 at roughly a third of revenue. Assistants meant to work across dozens of markets add another layer, because they need native speakers rather than translated English, and tone and idiom rarely survive machine translation intact. None of this is bulk work. Quality decides the ceiling, quietly When labels involve judgment, two careful people will sometimes disagree, and how a team handles that disagreement sets the ceiling on the model. Teams that treat annotation as a checkbox find out late, after a model has learned the noise in its data. A vision system trained on loose boxes places its own boxes loosely. A reward model trained on rushed preference data learns to prefer answers that look confident over answers that are correct. The failure is quiet. It is set before anyone runs the evaluation that would reveal it, which is why serious teams watch inter-annotator agreement the way they watch a production metric. Can models label their own data? The obvious move is to let a strong model label the data for the next one. For easy cases, that works, and it cuts the human load on routine tasks. Large models can pre-label, cluster similar examples, and flag likely edge cases for review. But training a model mostly on another model’s output has limits. Feed a system too much of its own synthetic data and small errors compound instead of averaging out. A model also cannot reliably flag its own blind spots; if it could see them, they would not be blind. Human review remains the step that catches the case the model was never going to catch on its own. What this means for teams building models The practical shift is easy to state and easy to underrate. Annotation is not a line item to push to the cheapest vendor and forget. It sits alongside architecture and evaluation as a place where a large share of a model’s behavior is decided, which is why Meta was willing to spend $14 billion to secure a seat in it. The caveat is that none of this is settled. Automated labeling keeps improving, synthetic data will cover more routine cases each year, and the market is full of vendors who promise judgment and deliver crowdwork. The teams that pull ahead will be the ones who can tell the difference, and who treat the people labeling their data as part of the model rather than a cost to grind down. Author: AIJ Thought Leader

data.title: The $2.5 Billion Referee: Who Graded the AI Graders
data.ai_summary: UniPat AI, a nine-month-old company that designs tests for AI models, was valued at $2.5 billion with Alibaba leading a $300 million round. The company sells benchmarking data and credibility, but its independence as a referee is questioned since it is owned by multiple AI labs. The deal signals value shifting from models to measurement and data.
data.author: Arjun Varmafollow
data.full_text:
A nine-month-old company you can't buy just got priced at $2.5 billion. UniPat AI makes tests for other AI models. Alibaba is reportedly leading a $300 million round in it, with Tencent and earlier backers joining, and the financing is expected to close soon. The founder, Li Kuan, is a Peking University PhD student who used to work in Alibaba's own Tongyi lab.

The first thing to notice is what the money buys. UniPat designs realistic scenarios that measure whether AI models can do real work, then sells the training and benchmarking data it creates to researchers and businesses. Its benchmarks cover coding agents, browser agents, and visual reasoning, and it builds small models of its own for prediction and scientific research. The market has already cast a vote: American labs have started citing UniPat's benchmarks in their own work. That is the closest thing this field has to a customer.

So why does anyone pay a fortune for a scorekeeper? Because the AI industry is running on tests nobody fully trusts. Models are graded on leaderboards that can be gamed, and a model can post a 99.9% score while failing at a real task. Data is the bottleneck too — human-generated examples are scarce and expensive. One widely used benchmark found that frontier models completed fewer than a quarter of expert-authored tasks on the first attempt. That gap between a great demo and reliable work is now a real business. Mercor, which sources expert reviewers, pushed annualized revenue past $2 billion and is negotiating a valuation near $20 billion. Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in data-labeling firm Scale AI.

But notice where most of that money is not going. The pure leaders — things like Artificial Analysis and Chatbot Arena — are largely free. The billions are flowing to the companies supplying the data and the humans behind the tests, not to the verdicts themselves. UniPat straddles the two: it sells data, and it sells the credibility of being the referee. Whether that credibility survives is the whole question.

Here is the contradiction the deal can't paper over. For an evaluation lab, independence is the product. A grader owned by the team it grades is worth less as a grader. There is a clean precedent for how this breaks: after Meta bought a stake in Scale AI, the frontier labs that compete with Meta — Google, OpenAI, xAI — stopped using it. One owner, and the referee lost the trust of everyone else.

UniPat runs the opposite structure, and I suspect it is deliberate. Instead of being owned by one contestant, it is being bought by several at once: AlibabaBABA-- leads the round, Tencent is in, and money linked to ByteDance has backed the lab on the side. A referee owned jointly by reigning teams is the classic answer to "who watches the watchmen" — no single owner can steer it, because the others would catch it. That is the genuinely interesting bet here, and it is not obvious it works.

The test is whether UniPat keeps credibility with the labs that don't own it. American researchers have cited its benchmarks without holding equity in it. The moment those citations dry up — because the owners' rivals no longer trust the score — the $2.5 billion stops making sense. That is a falsifiable claim about the future, and it is the one thing worth watching.

For an ordinary investor there is no direct ticket: UniPat is private and young. The deal matters a different way. It is a signal that value in AI is sliding from the models to the measurement-and-data layer around them — the thing that decides what "good" means as models become interchangeable. And it says something about Alibaba specifically, which has quietly assembled a web of AI bets: a 36% stake in model-maker Moonshot AI, whose Kimi topped global rankings, a 3-D startup called Vast, and now a stake in the referee. It is doing all of this while its own shares trade near 52-week lows, down roughly 25% this year. The spending is a strategic wager on the whole stack; the market's problem with the stock has little to do with strategy.

The useful way to hold the story is the contradiction, not the headline. Anyone can pay for a grader. The hard part is being a grader that survives being bought. So ask it like a referee question: whoever owns you, can the losing team still accept your call?

data.title: Meta's chief AI officer wants 13-year-olds spending "all" their time learning this one skill
data.ai_summary: Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang told teenagers to spend all their time learning to code with AI tools, calling it vibe-coding. He cited the 10,000-hour mastery rule and said AI will write most code within five years. Wang left Scale AI to join Meta after a $14.3 billion investment.
data.author: TOI Education; Sep
data.full_text:
Meta's chief AI officer has one message for teenagers: put down everything else and start learning to code with artificial intelligence (AI).
Alexandr Wang, 28, who co-founded Scale AI before dropping out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), said on the
TBPN podcast earlier this month that young people should treat what's known as vibe-coding, using AI tools to write code from plain English instructions, as close to a full-time pursuit.
"If you are, like, 13 years old, you should spend all of your time vibe-coding," Wang said. "That's how you should live your life."
Why he wants teens starting early
Wang's advice leans on the idea that early, sustained practice builds an edge that's hard to catch up on later. He pointed to the familiar theory that mastery takes around 10,000 hours, and said teenagers who put in that kind of time with AI coding tools now would come out ahead.
"That's a huge advantage," Wang said.
Tools such as Replit and Cursor have made this kind of learning accessible even to people with no coding background, letting them build apps and websites just by describing what they want. Google CEO
Sundar Pichai said in June that he had used AI to vibe-code a webpage himself.
AI is already doing the job at Microsoft and Google
Wang's comments come as AI takes on a growing share of the coding work at large technology companies. At Microsoft and Google, AI tools reportedly write up to 30% of the code used in company projects, a shift Wang said has reshaped how he sees his own profession.
"It's impossible to understate the degree to which I've been radicalized by AI coding," he said. "I think that fundamentally, the role of an engineer is very different now than it was before."
He predicted that within five years, AI models will be able to produce most of the code written for real projects, including, in his words, "literally all the code" he has ever written himself.
A track record built on skipping convention
Wang left MIT after his freshman year to start Scale AI, a data-labeling company for AI training, in 2016, and ran it as chief executive officer (CEO) for nearly a decade. That run made him the world's youngest self-made billionaire, with a net worth of $2 billion, according to Forbes. In June, Wang announced he was leaving Scale AI to join Meta after the company invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI for a 49% stake and access to its talent, including Wang. The deal roughly doubled Scale AI's valuation, from $14 billion to $29 billion.
He isn't the only one saying it
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a similar case in June, saying it no longer matters whether someone has ever learned to code in the traditional sense, since natural language now works as a programming language of its own for prompting AI.
For Wang, the point for teenagers is simple: the sooner AI coding becomes second nature, the better placed they'll be for a job market it's already reshaping.

data.title: The 'pocket money' of 500,000 people is gone.
data.ai_summary: Amazon announced the shutdown of Mechanical Turk, its 21-year-old data labeling platform, effective September 30, 2026. The platform, which had over 500,000 workers, is being replaced by professional data labeling firms like Scale AI and Mercor, which have higher valuations. The article notes that AI now performs many labeling tasks, reducing demand for such workers.
data.author: 投中网

naics_codes.name: Administrative and Support and Waste Management and Remediation Services
Administrative and Support and Waste Management and Remediation Services

data.full_text: Not long ago, Amazon wrote a line on the official website of Mechanical Turk, officially announcing the shutdown of this artificial data labeling platform that has been established for 21 years, which also means the end of an era. "We regularly evaluate our projects, tools, and services, and make adjustments accordingly. After evaluation, we have decided to close AWS Mechanical Turk, effective September 30, 2026." It is worth noting that at its peak, Mechanical Turk had over 500,000 registered workers, and its labeling tasks were distributed to more than 190 countries. It taught humans to draw boxes for machines, transcribe speech, and determine whether a tweet contained racial discrimination, and it also conveniently invented the term "gig economy." A platform that makes people "pretend to be machines" The original intention of Mechanical Turk was very simple. In 2005, there were too many products in Amazon's e-commerce catalog that needed to be classified, deduplicated, and corrected, and the algorithms at that time could not handle such tasks that required common sense. Therefore, Bezos proposed an idea: instead of waiting for algorithms to become stronger, it would be better to break down these tasks that are easy for humans but difficult for machines into fragments, distribute them to the idle workforce around the world via the internet, and then use APIs to bring them back into the program, making it look like a piece of computable power. After that, we saw tasks being broken down into micro-tasks of a few seconds, priced at a few cents, posted online, and allowing anyone in front of any computer in the world to grab them. This process is fast, cheap, and flexible, requiring no hiring of anyone and no signing of contracts. As for its name—Mechanical Turk—it comes from an 18th-century scam. "Mechanical Turk" was an automatic machine that claimed to play chess, but in the end, people discovered that there was actually a real chess player hidden inside the box. Bezos decided to name this artificial labeling platform after it and unabashedly described it as "artificial artificial intelligence," meaning that on the surface it is AI, but inside the box, it is all humans. However, no one expected that this platform would even become the foundation of the entire machine learning renaissance. Although for a considerable period, it was indeed just the infrastructure of one company. Amazon used its own workers to label product data for its retail website, and later this human network also supported the SageMaker machine learning service. But gradually, MTurk became the default experimental field for academia, where researchers in behavioral economics, psychology, and sociology used it to recruit subjects, distribute questionnaires, and conduct behavioral experiments. In many papers, it would honestly state, "This study recruited subjects through Amazon Mechanical Turk." Here, we must mention an experience of Fei-Fei Li when she was working on ImageNet. Initially, she chose to hire undergraduates for labeling at $10 per hour, but at that speed, it would take 19 years to label the entire dataset. Later, she chose to use MTurk, and as a result, from 2008 to 2010, nearly 50,000 workers from 167 countries labeled 14 million images in two years, improving efficiency by nearly 10 times. In the following decade, almost every AI breakthrough was backed by MTurk, with sentiment analysis, speech recognition, content moderation, and autonomous driving scenarios hiding pedestrian boxes drawn by humans. Reports indicate that in 2022, when OpenAI was refining the training data for ChatGPT, it was still using this platform for quality control. It also supported another thing, the "gig economy," which as an academic concept directly stems from research on MTurk. Phil Jones wrote in "The Post-Work Era" that the platform advertised "work anytime, anywhere," but workers had to spend several hours each day refreshing pages, waiting, and grabbing tasks, often ending up with nothing after tasks were unjustly rejected. Just as Bezos proudly admired his invention, a crisis was quietly approaching. The turning point in this track was not a specific date, but the emergence of a new batch of players. We saw that after 2016, data labeling companies with different backgrounds and entry points were established one after another. They did the same thing that MTurk failed to do, upgrading data labeling from a gig that anyone could do to a production process that required screening, assessment, quality standards, and professional tools. They recruited more reliable workers, provided better tools, and delivered cleaner data. In contrast, MTurk was almost left to fend for itself, and its business could not deliver high-quality data comparable to the new players. The most ironic scene occurred in the last leg of its life cycle. In 2023, a study by the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL) found that at that time, 30% to 50% of MTurk workers were already using large language models to complete tasks. In other words, on a platform that made humans pretend to be machines, in the end, humans used machines to pretend to be humans. Same track, different fates The exit of MTurk is not a contraction of the industry, but an upgrade of competition and a divergence of paths. During the same period, some saw their market value drop by 99%, while others saw their valuation double in a year. This track has not lacked star companies in the past two years, and wealth creation myths have been continuously staged, as we have written more than once. The most prominent among them is Scale AI. In June last year, Meta acquired 49% of Scale AI for $14.3 billion, raising its valuation from $14 billion to about $29 billion. In fact, Scale AI's early approach was somewhat similar to MTurk; they hired low-paid contractors to label datasets for AI training and quickly achieved breakthroughs in the autonomous driving field. Fortunately, they quickly transformed into a professional service provider focused on providing large-scale data labeling. At the same time, facing the problem of data scarcity in some industries, Scale AI actively expanded downstream and ventured into the field of synthetic data generation. Another newly rising star, Mercor, has also attracted attention because it has hit the wind of the times. Three entrepreneurs born in the 2000s took only three years to achieve a company valuation of $20 billion. Initially, Mercor was just an engineering outsourcing platform that used AI to screen resumes, and its first client paid $500 per week, of which $350 went to the engineer. Later, it recruited and managed tens of thousands of industry experts worldwide, accelerating AI training through carefully selected domain-specific knowledge. Clients only need to upload task descriptions, and the system can assemble interdisciplinary labeling, evaluation, and RLHF training teams within hours. Therefore, Mercor's success stems from its change in the business model of data labeling, not relying on traditional price differences, but on the ability to organize human expertise. Of course, these two companies somewhat represent survivor bias, as many others have not only MTurk have declined in the past two years. Appen, an Australian listed company, was once seen as an industrial-scale version of the MTurk model, mainly relying on global crowdsourcing, low-cost labor, and undertaking evaluation and labeling for search giants. In August 2020, its stock price once reached a historical high of AUD 41.49, with a market value of about $4.3 billion, but just four years later, following the termination of its contract with Google, the company's stock price quickly fell to AUD 0.26, with a market value evaporating by over 99%. The Chinese market has not been spared either. Traditional data labeling companies have struggled to command high prices and have not produced giant companies like Scale AI and Mercor. However, recently, a batch of data companies emerging from large model companies, which have resources, channels, and business understanding, have become star underwater projects in the primary market. On the policy front, in 2025, four departments jointly issued a document planning for the data labeling industry to achieve an average annual compound growth rate of over 20% by 2027, and included the "AI pre-labeling + human review" human-machine collaboration model in the official discourse. In April this year, the National Data Bureau also issued a document requiring the establishment of an industry expert certification mechanism. Various enterprises have also reacted accordingly. Major companies no longer call their positions data labeling but instead refer to them as data alchemists, AI question experts, etc. Reports indicate that in a major company, the team in a self-built base in a third-tier city had not finished training, and the demand had already changed to requiring master's or doctoral degrees. More concrete changes are hidden in the job descriptions, with master's-level positions all squeezed into large model evaluation, algorithm support, and overseas multilingual directions. For example, JD.com is recruiting for labeling in French, German, and Dutch, with a requirement of a level eight proficiency, and another major company is offering a monthly salary of 100,000 yuan to recruit doctors from top hospitals for labeling. Finally, returning to the shutdown of MTurk, AI does not no longer need humans to label data, but it does not need repetitive labor that anyone can do. This is somewhat sad to say; the workers of MTurk labeled the training data for AI, and AI learned new skills, thus the workers were eliminated. This inevitably reminds one of the metaphor mentioned at the beginning, the 18th-century Turkish robot, which deceived the world for decades with the real chess player hidden in the cabinet, and now the cabinet has been opened, and there is no longer a need for that real person; the machine has finally learned to play chess by itself.

data.title: Luca Del Vecchio, Surya Midha, Alexandr Wang, Brendan Foody, Adarsh Hiremath: Meet the 15 billionaires who became rich before 30
data.ai_summary: Forbes' 2026 list shows 35 billionaires under 30 with a combined $92.4 billion, including 12 self-made. Mercor's three 22-year-old founders each hold $2.2 billion, while heirs to Luxottica and Boehringer Ingelheim lead the inherited wealth.
data.author: Jay Hilotin
data.full_text: Luca Del Vecchio, Surya Midha, Alexandr Wang, Brendan Foody, Adarsh Hiremath: Meet the 15 billionaires who became rich before 30 Inside the dynasties and AI startups minting billionaires before age 30 Last updated: September 07, 2026 | 07:41 Jay Hilotin , Senior Assistant Editor 8 MIN READ Add as a preferred source on Google World's top billionaires under-30: Clockwise (from top left): Katharina Andresen, Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio and Alexandra Andresen, Brendan Foody, Surya Midha, Adarsh Hiremath and Alexandr Wang. File A new generation of billionaires is reshaping the global wealth rankings, with AI startups, pharmaceuticals, luxury goods and inherited family empires producing extraordinary fortunes before their owners turn 30. According to Forbes, 35 people under 30 appeared on its 2026 World’s Billionaires list, with a combined fortune of $92.4 billion as of March 1, 2026. Twelve (12) were self-made. Disruptors Mercor's three founders are particularly notable because they became billionaires at 22, surpassing Mark Zuckerberg 's age when he first reached billionaire status. The biggest disruption has emerged from artificial intelligence (AI), which has created a new billionaire class Surya Midha, Brendan Foody and Adarsh Hiremath, all 22, each have an estimated $2.2 billion fortune from Mercor, their AI recruiting company. Forbes reported that Midha is the youngest self-made billionaire in the world, edging out his two cofounders by a matter of months. Alexandr Wang , 29, remains another major AI success story. His fortune was built through Scale AI, which Forbes valued at billions of dollars following Meta's acquisition of a 49% stake. Wang subsequently became Meta's chief AI officer. Other young self-made billionaires include Cursor cofounders Aman Sanger and Michael Truell, as well as Lovable cofounder Fabian Hedin. Here are the 15 richest, ranked by estimated net worth: #1. Luca Del Vecchio — $6.8 billion, age 24 Luca Del Vecchio is one of the heirs to the Italian eyewear empire created by his late father, Leonardo Del Vecchio, founder of Luxottica. Luca inherited a 12.5% stake in Delfin, the family's Luxembourg-based holding company, which owns a major interest in EssilorLuxottica, the world's largest eyewear company and owner of brands including Ray-Ban and Persol. Luca is not known for holding an operational role at EssilorLuxottica. His fortune is therefore largely inherited rather than generated through entrepreneurship. #2. Clemente Del Vecchio — $6.8 billion, age 21 Clemente Del Vecchio, the younger brother of Luca, inherited the same substantial family stake following the death of their father in 2022. At just 21, he is among the world's youngest billionaires and one of its richest people under 30. His estimated 12.5% interest in Delfin provides exposure not only to EssilorLuxottica but also to other major European investments held by the family. Clemente's wealth illustrates the enormous scale of the generational transfer of the Del Vecchio fortune. #3. Maximilian von Baumbach — $6.6 billion, age 28 Maximilian von Baumbach is the eldest of four young siblings who inherited stakes in Boehringer Ingelheim , one of the world's largest privately held pharmaceutical companies. The German company was founded in 1885 and has remained under family ownership for generations. Unlike publicly traded pharmaceutical fortunes, the family's wealth is tied to its private ownership structure. Maximilian's billionaire status comes principally from that inheritance. His position among the world's richest people under 30 demonstrates how private, multigenerational industrial and pharmaceutical businesses can create enormous family fortunes. #4. Katharina von Baumbach — $6.6 billion, age 26 Katharina von Baumbach is the only woman among the four young von Baumbach heirs on Forbes' under-30 billionaire list. She inherited her fortune through the family's ownership of Boehringer Ingelheim, the German pharmaceutical giant founded in the 19th century. The company remains privately controlled rather than being listed on a stock exchange, making the family's wealth unusual among major pharmaceutical fortunes. Katharina's billionaire status reflects her ownership stake in the family business rather than a personal startup or operating career. #5. Franz von Baumbach — $6.6 billion, age 24 Franz von Baumbach is another member of the younger generation of the family that controls Boehringer Ingelheim. Founded in Ingelheim, Germany, in 1885, the pharmaceutical company has grown into a global healthcare business while remaining family-owned. Franz inherited his billionaire-level stake as part of the family's succession structure. His fortune underscores the continuing importance of private family enterprises in producing young billionaires: unlike the newest technology fortunes, his wealth was accumulated over more than a century before being transferred to his generation. #6. Johannes von Baumbach — $6.6 billion, age 20 At only 20, Johannes von Baumbach is one of the world's youngest billionaires and the youngest member of the four-person von Baumbach sibling group. His fortune comes from the family's ownership of Boehringer Ingelheim, the German pharmaceutical company. The business has been led by family members for generations, with Johannes' uncle Hubertus von Baumbach serving as chairman. Beyond his inheritance, Johannes has reportedly pursued competitive skiing in Austria. His story highlights the extraordinary wealth transferred to the youngest generation of established European industrial families. #7. Kevin David Lehmann — $4.9 billion, age 23 Kevin David Lehmann became a billionaire through Germany's dm-drogerie markt drugstore chain. His father transferred a 50% stake in the company to him in 2017, when Lehmann was only 14. The family's connection to dm dates to 1974, shortly after the retailer was founded in 1973. Today, dm is Germany's leading drugstore chain. Lehmann's fortune is a striking example of wealth being transferred unusually early: he became the nominal owner of a multibillion-dollar stake while still a teenager. #8. Firoz Mistry — $3.1 billion, age 29 Firoz Mistry is an heir to the sprawling Tata business empire through the family's ownership of Tata Sons. He and his younger brother Zahan inherited 4.6% stakes in Tata Sons following their father Cyrus Mistry's death in a car accident in 2022. Tata Sons is the holding company behind a vast multinational group whose businesses span automobiles, technology, steel, consumer products and luxury goods. The Mistry family also controls the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, one of India's major construction and infrastructure conglomerates. #9. Zahan Mistry — $3.1 billion, age 27 Zahan Mistry shares his brother Firoz's inheritance from the Tata conglomerate. Following their father's death, the brothers received stakes of about 4.6% each in Tata Sons. Their family also has deep roots in India's Shapoorji Pallonji Group, a construction and engineering empire dating back to the 19th century. Zahan's wealth therefore combines exposure to one of India's most recognizable corporate groups with the family's private business interests. The brothers are part of a younger generation expected to help manage the family's enormous corporate legacy. #10. Alexandr Wang — $3.2 billion, age 29 Alexandr Wang represents a very different route to billionaire status. He founded Scale AI, a company that provides data and AI infrastructure used to train artificial-intelligence systems. Wang became the world's youngest self-made billionaire before being overtaken by Mercor's younger founders. In 2025, Meta agreed to acquire a 49% stake in Scale AI in a deal valuing the company at about $29 billion, while Wang became Meta's chief AI officer. His rise illustrates how rapidly AI has created immense paper wealth for young technology entrepreneurs. #11. Alexandra Andresen — $2.5 billion, age 29 Norwegian billionaire Alexandra Andresen inherited her fortune from the family behind Ferd, an investment company with holdings in real estate, finance and private Nordic businesses. The family fortune originated in a cigarette business that her father sold in 2005 before shifting the family's focus toward investment. Andresen and her older sister are involved at the board level of Ferd. Outside business, she has a strong equestrian background and was a three-time Norwegian junior champion in dressage. She continues to own and operate a horse-breeding stable in Oslo. #12. Remi Dassault — $2.4 billion, age 24 Remi Dassault belongs to France's powerful Dassault industrial dynasty. His great-grandfather, Marcel Dassault, began the family fortune by developing aircraft propellers during World War I before building the business that became Dassault Aviation. Remi inherited major stakes after his father, Olivier Dassault, died in a helicopter crash in 2021. His holdings include an estimated 4.1% stake in Dassault Aviation and about 2.5% in software company Dassault Systèmes. The family also owns media, wine and aviation interests. #13. Surya Midha — $2.2 billion, age 22 Surya Midha is one of the three founders of Mercor, an AI recruiting company that helps major technology companies and AI laboratories find specialized talent and train AI models. Born in California to a family with roots in India, Midha became a national-level debate champion during high school. He founded Mercor in 2023 with Brendan Foody and Adarsh Hiremath. Private investors valued the company at $10 billion in 2025, making the three founders billionaires at 22. Midha is the youngest self-made billionaire on Forbes' 2026 list. #14. Brendan Foody — $2.2 billion, age 22 Brendan Foody is the CEO and cofounder of Mercor, the AI recruiting startup he launched in 2023 with Surya Midha and Adarsh Hiremath. The three founders met through their high-school debate networks and later became Thiel Fellows, a program supporting young entrepreneurs. Foody attended Georgetown University but dropped out after launching Mercor. Before Mercor, he had already founded two startups focused on software development. The company's rapid rise and $10 billion private valuation turned Foody into one of the world's youngest self-made billionaires. #15. Adarsh Hiremath — $2.2 billion, age 22 Adarsh Hiremath is Mercor's cofounder and chief technology officer, completing the trio of 22-year-old entrepreneurs who became the world's youngest self-made billionaires. Hiremath and Midha were high-school debate teammates before building Mercor with Foody in 2023. The company uses AI to connect companies with specialized workers and help major AI laboratories train their models. Mercor's $10 billion valuation in 2025 gave each founder an estimated 22% stake and transformed a startup founded only two years earlier into a multibillion-dollar fortune. What the list reveals The ranking shows a sharp divide between inherited wealth and new technology fortunes. Most of the top positions are occupied by heirs to century-old European and Asian business dynasties, while the self-made billionaires come overwhelmingly from artificial intelligence.
